Seeing Ma Ming berate Ma Yu, he followed along and said, "Do not blame him. Your squire is an honest man, and blaming him is useless. Go and call that old gentleman Wang out, and let me question him and see what his reason is." Having spoken, he called Ma Xing to go and bring him. Ma Xing was gone only a short while when he brought the old gentleman to the front of the hall. He did not exchange courtesies with anyone, and no one paid him the least regard. At the sight of him Ma Ming laughed aloud and said, "I wondered which Mr. Wang it was; so it is that beggarly lone old man." Ma Wenkui said to Master Chongyang, "You old fellow have begged in our parts for several years, and we have never heard that you had any ability. We do not know what our squire saw in you to take you into the house, where you have clothes and food; that is quite enough. You should have kept to your place and lived out your remaining years in peace. Why have you deluded my nephew and made him renounce the family fortune to you? You are a man of fifty or sixty; you cannot be wholly without sense. Where under heaven is there such a principle? Do you not fear to be laughed at when you say such things?"

When Ma Wenkui had finished, Master Chongyang answered, "All my life I have had no ability; it is only that I have been frightened by poverty, and so I told him to let me have this family fortune, that I might live a few easy years. Let them laugh or not as they please." Before he had finished, Ma Fu and Ma Gui sprang forward and spat (
cuì

, spitting at a man to show contempt) several times in Master Chongyang's face, saying, "You shameless old fellow! A wry-mouthed girl wanting to wear a phoenix crown, a weasel wanting to eat swan's flesh! You have lived fifty or sixty years to no purpose, and now you speak such shameless words; it makes one furious." Ma Fu said to Ma Gui, "Let us not make a clamor; the best plan is simply to drive him out of the village." So saying, they were about to lay hands on him, when Ma Zhao came forward and blocked them, saying, "There is no need to drive him out. Have pity on him as a lone old man; since our squire has kept him, let him be. Only let the squire not renounce the estate, and that is all." Only then did Ma Fu and Ma Gui hold their hands. Squire Ma whispered something or other into the tribute scholar Ma's ear, and Ma Long said to the company, "You youngsters need not make such a clamor; go home, each of you. I have my own decision to make: if I do not let him renounce it, how would he dare?" This old tribute scholar was the senior elder of the whole Ma clan, and who dared disobey him? So each went home.

Squire Ma privately kept back Ma Long, Ma Wenkui, and Ma Zhao, invited them into the study to sit down, and entertained them with wine and food. The old tribute scholar sat at the head; Scholar Ma sat at the lower end to keep him company; the imperial-college scholar Ma sat on the left and Squire Ma on the right. They had no sooner sat down than servants came and went passing cups and bowls, filling the flagon and pouring the wine, with fine dishes and delicacies beyond telling. When three rounds of wine had passed, Squire Ma rose to his feet and said, "My third grandfather, my second uncle, and my elder brother are all here. I, Ma Yu, have a matter on my mind that I wish to discuss with my third grandfather and my second uncle." Scholar Ma said, "Whatever you have to say, say it; we will all turn it over together." Squire Ma said, "Would I really renounce my family property to Wang Chongyang? I would only let him keep watch over it for me for a few years, so that I may get a little leisure." Ma Zhao said, "Letting him keep watch is no great matter; but why draw up a deed of renunciation?" Squire Ma said, "Elder brother, you do not understand. This is nothing but a temporary expedient: I want to make him wholeheartedly and sincerely keep watch for me, so that I can be at ease and he will not grow slack." Ma Wenkui said, "Your reasoning I do not understand; tell it to me slowly." Squire Ma said, "Second uncle, hear your nephew out. It is only that your nephew is much afflicted with illness, and your nephew's wife too is often troubled with dizziness, so that she finds it hard to manage affairs. For a long time I have wished to find an honest, loyal man to run things for me. Happily heaven has answered my wish, and this old gentleman Wang has come, a man of the utmost honesty and loyalty. I had a mind to hand the estate over to him to manage, and so I said to him, 'Manage this household well, and treat it as though it were your own estate; do not be of two minds.' The old gentleman did not know how to take a hint, and asked me straight out, 'You tell me to treat this fortune as my own; do you mean to renounce it to me?' Seeing him talk such foolish talk, I answered him in his own foolish vein: 'Renounce it to you? Renounce it to you, then; what does it matter?' It was plainly a joke, but he took it for the truth and demanded that I invite the clan heads to witness and draw up a written deed of renunciation for him. I reckon that he is a lone man with no close kin, no relatives or friends; even if I renounce it to him, he cannot carry it off anywhere. Besides, he is advanced in years; how many more years can he live? Let me draw up a deed for him and win his goodwill, so that he will manage things for me with single-hearted devotion, while I enjoy some leisure and nurse my illness. When he dies, the fortune comes back to me. What loss is there in it? I beg my second uncle to decide for me and bring this matter to completion."

Scholar Ma said, "The clan is large, and I cannot decide alone. Ask your third grandfather and see what he says." Before Ma Wenkui had finished speaking, the old tribute scholar Ma Long shook his head and said, "I do not meddle with the affairs of a younger generation, and I too cannot decide. Let us see what Ma Zhao says." The imperial-college scholar Ma said, "With the clan head present, how dare I presume to decide for myself?" Squire Ma knew that empty words would get him nowhere, so he went inside and fetched out a certain treasure, waved it once before their eyes, and bewitched them all; they had no choice but to decide. And what, you ask, was this treasure?
Gleaming white, both hard and firm, with it a hundred things are done;
Bright and shining, round or square, without it nothing can be won.

Now Squire Ma gave each of the three men a share of this treasure. Having got the treasure, their eyes narrowed to slits with laughter, and they could not help changing their tune. The tribute scholar Ma said to Scholar Ma, "Ma Yu explained it clearly enough just now: it is only a matter of using the deed of renunciation to tie the old fellow's heart, so that he will devote himself to managing the household. That is a harmless thing." Scholar Ma said, "Though it be a temporary expedient, everyone must lend a hand." The imperial-college scholar Ma said, "So long as the third grandfather and the second uncle are willing to decide, I will go and pacify the rest of them myself." Ma Wenkui said, "If it comes to that, your third grandfather and I will make the decision between us; but how will you pacify the clansmen?" Ma Zhao whispered a few words in his ear, and Ma Wenkui said joyfully, "Excellent, excellent! Said that way, why fear they will not submit?" Then he rose and said to Ma Yu, "Set your mind at ease; I guarantee the thing will be done." But how was the deed of renunciation to be drawn up? Read on.
When silver is at hand, great matters are done; why fret that the deed cannot be drawn?

blocks.text: 07. Bribing the Clan Head, Ma Yu Signs the Deed of Renunciation; Discussing the Mystic Work, Chongyang Transmits the True Cultivation

inline.s: The running waters hurry on, so do not delay;
Fame and profit entangle like a snare; at the ten-thousand-fathom cliff let go your hold, and with no thread attached no demon will grow bold.

Now Squire Ma, following Sun Yuanzhen's counsel, had bribed the three men of consequence in the clan. Ma Wenkui then had Ma Zhao speak to the clansmen: "Ma Yu's talk of renouncing his property was only a stratagem." The clansmen asked, "What stratagem is it?" Ma Zhao answered, "The stratagem of keeping a tiger to guard the mountain." The clansmen asked again, "And what is his purpose in using such a stratagem?" Ma Zhao said, "Ma Yu wants to enjoy leisure and quiet, so he keeps the old man to be a slave that guards his hoard." The clansmen asked, "How do you know he keeps him as a slave to guard the hoard?" Ma Zhao said, "Ma Yu sees that the old fellow is an honest, loyal man and wants to keep him to manage the estate, but he fears he will not put his heart into it. So he pretends to renounce the property to him. The old man takes it for truth and demands a deed. Ma Yu reckons that if he does not draw up a deed, the old man will not watch over it diligently; therefore he invites us to be witnesses and writes him a deed, to tie his heart and make him guard it with all sincerity. Is that not keeping a tiger to guard the mountain?" The clansmen said, "If it is renounced to him, the property is his; why should he not guard it?" Ma Zhao said, "He cannot take away a single hair of it. How can you call it his?" The clansmen said, "How do you know he cannot take away a single hair?" Ma Zhao said, "He is a lone old man from a distant place with no kin. And at his great age he cannot eat much or wear much. When his eyes close he will go empty-handed as he came empty-handed, and the estate will still return to its former master. The old fellow will have kept watch for nothing — is he not a slave guarding a hoard?" The clansmen all laughed at this. Ma Zhao then tempted them with profit: "When the old man dies the property still returns to Ma Yu. Ma Yu has no son or heir — why worry that it will not fall into the hands of us sons and nephews? Now let us go with the current and do a false kindness, granting him his wish. I see that the old gentleman is a man of feeling and honor; if we bring this affair off, then in days to come, if we are short of anything, we can borrow from him. As the saying goes, 'Leave a thread of courtesy today, and you will meet again with ease tomorrow.'" Hearing Ma Zhao's words, the clansmen all gladly consented.
Words need not be many, as we know;
A single phrase can lay the billows low; yet once a bribe has bought a private end, even good words are twisted to a wrong end.

Now when Ma Zhao saw that the clansmen had agreed, he appointed the next day for all to assemble. On the following day the clansmen came to Squire Ma's house, where they found the old tribute scholar Ma Long seated in the hall with Master Wang Chongyang, laughing and chatting, gesturing and pointing, discoursing of heaven and earth, in the warmest intimacy. Ma Wenkui told Squire Ma to prepare many tables and set out wine and dishes. When all the clansmen had arrived, he spoke: "All the elders and youngers, high and low of the clan, are here. Ma Yu is willing to renounce his property to the venerable Mr. Wang Chongyang. Do you consent or not?" These men had all been persuaded by Ma Zhao — who among them would not consent? At once they answered with one voice, "We are all willing; we have no objection." Ma Wenkui then had Ma Yu write out the deed of renunciation and read it to the assembly. Ma Wenkui took it and handed it to Ma Zhao, who read aloud:

I, Ma Yu, the maker of this deed of renunciation, do hereby renounce into the name of the venerable Mr. Wang Chongyang, to hold and manage at his own free pleasure, all the gardens, fields, houses, silver, goods, household servants, young attendants, maidservants, bondwomen, furniture, farm implements, and utensils left to me by my forefathers and my father. No man of the Ma clan has any objection. After renouncing them, Ma Yu may not retract or repent. Lest word of mouth be without proof, this deed is made as evidence. Clan heads: Ma Long, Ma Wenkui, Ma Wenxian, Ma Wende, Ma Wenyu. Witnesses: Ma Zhao, Ma Ming, Ma Jian, Ma Zhen. Maker of the deed: Ma Yu. This is the truth."

When Ma Zhao had finished reading the deed, he handed it back to Ma Yu. Ma Yu presented it with both hands to Master Chongyang. The master received it and at once ordered the feast to be spread. They ate great chunks of meat and drank great cups of wine, feasting until they were drunk and full, and only then dispersed. Reading to this point, the poet has a verse telling how Ma Yu in that year renounced his estate with such resolve, and therefore attained the Way so swiftly. The verse says:
His fortune gone, he longed for cultivation's way;
He kept no single thing — how could desire stay? That very day his wandering thoughts were done; therefore in years to come the Way he first had won.

Now when Squire Ma saw the clansmen disperse, he went into the inner chambers and said, "Had you not told me to do thus and so, my lady, how could this affair ever have been brought off?" Sun Yuanzhen laughed and said, "Whatever is done in accord with principle cannot fail." Squire Ma said, "It is done, but as for our seeking the Way — how shall we go about it?" Sun Yuanzhen said, "The seeking of the Way must advance by slow steps. Let the master rest for a few days, and then we shall go together to take him as our teacher." Squire Ma repeatedly said, "Excellent."

Let us leave aside Squire Ma and Sun Yuanzhen discussing the seeking of the Way, and speak again of Master Wang Chongyang, who had set his whole heart on gathering the world's cultivators here to cultivate truth and nurture their nature. Yet he feared that the neighbors round about might invent rumors and stir up trouble; so he could not but first bestow some benefits, so that every man would cherish his kindness and every one receive his grace, and thus be of use to him. Therefore he practiced generosity widely and bestowed much benevolence. Whether in cash or in rice, he constantly relieved the poor and the widowed, the orphaned and the childless. When any in the Ma clan were short of anything, he would help to make it up. Men who could not afford to marry he saw married; women who could not afford a dowry he saw wed. In every case of illness or burial he gave full assistance. If any borrowed and did not repay, he never went to demand it. This matched exactly what Ma Zhao had said of him — that he was a man of benevolence and honor. Thus within and without all was quiet, high and low were at peace, and however many people the master gathered here to discourse on the Way and talk of the mysteries, there was never a word of idle gossip. That the affair had a head and a tail, whole from beginning to end, was wholly the work of bestowing benefits on others. Let every man in authority, and every household of wealth and rank, beware of harboring a miserly heart and refusing to bestow benefits on others. A later reader, coming upon this passage, has a verse of lament:
No undertaking thrives on a miser's heart;
Idle talk springs up and will not depart; had Patriarch Wang not showered his bounty wide, how could he have enjoyed such peace on every side?

Now Master Wang Chongyang, having bestowed benefits abroad, also ordered matters within. He built more than ten thatched huts beside the rear garden, to serve as quiet retreats where cultivators might nurture their stillness. When all was ready, the master moved into the central hut to work at realization. One day Ma Yu and his wife Yuanzhen came together to the thatched hut, knelt down side by side, and sought the Way from the master. Master Chongyang said:

The Way is the path of awakening; it brings men back to the path of awakening and out of the wrong road. Yet one must proceed from the shallow to the deep and from the small to the great, in due order, and only then can there be achievement.

Whoever would learn the Way must first refine his nature. For nature is a thing of the prior heaven; it must be refined until it is perfectly round and brightly shining — only then does it have wondrous use. Now nature is joined to emotion; when nature and emotion are stirred they are like dragon and tiger running wild. If you do not refine them and make them submit, how can you strip away their wildness and return to emptiness?
In the way of refining nature, one must be utterly undifferentiated, knowing nothing and recognizing nothing, with no other and no self; only thus refined can one enter the Dharma.

When the way of subduing the dragon and taming the tiger has been practiced, one must further lock up the monkey mind and tether the horse of intent. What are called the monkey mind and the horse of intent mean that the mind is cunning as an ape and the intent runs like a wild horse; therefore one must tether and lock them, so that the ape has no chance to use its cunning and the horse no chance to race, and they return to stillness and stability.

The work of stillness and stability can seize the creative power of heaven and earth and the wondrous principle of yin and yang. If you can be still, ten thousand cares all melt away; if you can be stable, not a single thought arises. To follow the current is to be an ordinary man; to go against it is to be an immortal. You must let the mind hold not the least stray thought and not the slightest obstruction — empty and hollow, clinging to nothing, dim and dark, bearing no mark. This is what is called hanging by not a thread and unstained by a speck of dust. Such is the general outline of the Way.

There is more that is profound beyond all naming, to be grasped only by the heart and understood in the mind. When you have made progress, I will surely point it out to you. Ma Yu, I give you the Daoist name Danyang; Sun Yuanzhen, I give you the Daoist name Bu'er — meaning that you shall forever have no second heart."

When the names had been given, Ma Danyang and Sun Bu'er bowed together in thanks to their teacher and returned to the inner chambers. Sun Bu'er said to Ma Danyang, "Before we took the master and learned the Way, we were husband and wife; now that we have taken the same master and study the wondrous Way, we are companions on the Way. I shall call you senior brother, and you shall call me companion on the Way. Moreover, one who learns the Way must cut off fond love; we must live in separate rooms. You must not come to my room without leave, nor I to yours. If there is anything to discuss, send a maidservant to invite the other, and we shall meet in the front hall to talk it over." Ma Danyang said, "As you please; I have no objection. If you can be true-hearted, I can be true-minded. Even if I do not come to your room for a year or half a year, it does not matter." Having said this, Danyang called Ma Xing and had him carry blankets and bedding to the side room in front and set up a bed there. He took leave of Sun Bu'er and went to lodge in the side room. Later men wrote a verse telling how decisively this husband and wife parted rooms, and therefore attained the Way with ease.
The Great Way holds no love of passion's fire;
Cling to desire, and you shall miss the Way entire. Look at Patriarch Ma in those days gone by: husband and wife parted rooms with purpose high.

Now Sun Bu'er, after parting rooms with Ma Danyang, was unaware that half a month had passed. One day she sent a maidservant to invite Ma Danyang to go with her to the thatched hut to ask about the Way. Ma Danyang at once left the side room to meet Sun Bu'er. The two went together to the thatched hut, paid their respects to the master, and asked, "Yesterday you said, master, that nature is a thing of the prior heaven. May we ask what the prior heaven is like?" Master Chongyang said:

The prior heaven is the single undifferentiated qi. It has no color and no sound, no knowing and no recognizing. What can be made of it? If one says it is like something, then it is not the prior heaven. The very word 'like' loses the wondrous truth. It may not be spoken of as 'like'; to say the prior heaven is like anything at all is to cling to marks. Clinging to marks, one loses the substance of the prior heaven. If a man says the prior heaven is here, then here is already wrong; if a man says the prior heaven is there, then there too is not the meaning of prior heaven. Say it this way and that, and there is not a single thing; even the one word 'one' is only conjecture. Do not say the word 'one' is the prior heaven: the word 'one' is itself not it either. Since you now wish to know the principle of the prior heaven, I shall set it out for you in detail with my brush."
Having spoken, Master Chongyang took up his brush to set out the wondrous truth of the prior heaven. But how did he set it out? Read on.
Nature is the prior heaven's most numinous thing; refine the true nature, and that is the prior heaven.

blocks.text: 08. On the Wondrous Principle of the Prior Heaven's True One; Removing the Root of Demons, the Dharma Gate of Non-Duality

inline.s: Seek the immortal outside the mind, and the road goes wrong;
It is the moon in water, a flower in a mirror; do you know the wondrous principle of the prior heaven? It lies in the single mind alone — and that is glory enough.

Now Master Chongyang, expounding the Way to Danyang and Sun Bu'er, said, "Nature is originally one thing of the prior heaven, perfectly round and brightly shining; it has a name but no form, no knowing and no recognizing, hard to paint and hard to draw. What is it like? I will now for your sakes roughly sketch its likeness, and you must recognize it for yourselves." Having spoken, the master took up his brush and on a red-lacquered stool drew a circle ○, and within the circle dotted a point ⊙. When he had done, he said to Ma Danyang and Sun Bu'er, "Can you two understand this meaning?" Ma Danyang and Sun Bu'er answered together, "Our minds are dull, and we cannot understand this meaning. We beg you to instruct us."
Master Chongyang said:

This first circle is the image of the undifferentiated whole, before heaven and earth were divided and sun and moon distinguished; it is called the 'Ultimateless.' Non-being gives birth to being, and so within the circle a point is generated, and this is called the 'Great Ultimate.' That point gives birth to heaven, to earth, and to the ten thousand things. This Great Ultimate is born of the prior heaven, and this point is the one qi; hence it is called the one qi of the prior heaven.

This nature issues from the prior heaven; it issues before the body exists and remains after the body has perished. This single point of numinous nature is the root that is neither born nor destroyed; hence it is called the numinous root. This numinous root is possessed by everyone; it is only that ordinary men are blind to it — and being blind, they are deluded. Deluded about their own nature, they let false thoughts arise all at once, and wayward license (unrestrained and improper conduct) enters with those thoughts; they forever lose the prior heaven and never hear the Great Way. The sea of suffering is boundless — where is the shore?

Alas! Those who awaken to the Way are few, and few who practice truly inquire. The prior heaven may be verified everywhere; do not ask of the prior heaven with the human mind. If you ask of the prior heaven with the human mind, the prior heaven cannot be found at all; if you ask of the prior heaven relying on the mind of the Way, the prior heaven is right before your eyes. The human mind is the mind of one darkened, craving heart. The mind of the Way is the mind in which heavenly conscience has come to light. Once heavenly conscience has come to light, the prior heaven is gained without seeking.

Again, one must dispel (remove) illness. To dispel illness does not mean dispelling the illnesses of wind, cold, summer heat, and fever, but the illnesses of greed, anger, delusion, and craving. Once this illness is dispelled, a hundred illnesses will not arise; one may lengthen one's years and increase one's lifespan, become a Buddha or an immortal, a sage or a worthy. I now transmit this whole discipline to you; you should strive to practice it.

In the way of removing illness, one must remove its root. Find the root, and the illness is not hard to remove. These illnesses mostly come from greed, anger, delusion, and craving, and are also caused by wine, lust, wealth, and temper. Therefore one who cultivates must first remove wine, lust, wealth, and temper, doing away with outward afflictions; afterward he must cut off greed, anger, delusion, and craving, doing away with inward injury. Then the root of illness pulls itself out and the sick body heals of itself; thereafter the Great Way may be cultivated and long life obtained.

Now let us speak of the word 'wine.' There are those who know that wine harms the Way and vow to give it up. Yet when they see wine they still hold themselves back with relish in their abstinence. Then someone urges them, or they watch others play drinking games, and a wish to drink arises. They have not actually drunk; but once this wish arises it is as if they had drunk — this is the root of the wine illness. Whoever would remove it must remove it at the moment the wish arises; only then can the root be pulled out clean.

There are those who know that lust harms the Way and vow to give it up. Yet when they see beauty they still hold themselves back with thought after thought of abstinence. Then a lovely form offers charms, a slender figure shows its feeling, and their hearts are somewhat stirred, and a longing arises. They have not actually lain together; but once this feeling arises it is as if they had — this is the root of the lust illness. Whoever would remove it must remove it at the moment the feeling arises; only then can the root be wholly gone.

It is clear that the roots of the wine and lust illnesses are hidden within the heart and intent. In the way of removing the root of illness, one must first rectify the heart and make the intent sincere; then the root of illness is cut of itself. That the root is not cut is because heart and intent are not rectified. When heart and intent are unrectified, a single thought may arise: though one has not drunk, the intent has already drunk; though one has not lain together, the feeling has already done so. Before, there was no such thought; but being stirred from without, it moves within — like the moon in water: a stone on the bank strikes the water, and when the water moves the moon moves with it. Though there is no reality to it, the shadow already wavers, and the true Way cannot be attained.

If you seek the method of cutting the root, the Confucians have 'Look not at what is contrary to propriety, move not contrary to propriety' — seeing as though not seeing, hearing as though not hearing; the Buddhists have the saying 'Forget others, forget self, forget living beings'; the Daoists have the teaching 'Look at it and do not see it, listen to it and do not hear it.' All these can hoe out the root of the wine and lust illnesses.

As for the word 'wealth,' it is hard to speak of. There are those who, because the conditions for the Way are not yet ripe, make temporary calculations; there are those who, because their household is very poor, merely seek a living. Circumstances force them to it, and there is still the rule of overlooking the outward act and judging the original intention. But as for the rest — those who keep up appearances, who talk of pomp and display, of fine clothes and fine food, who talk of fields and villas, and those of cunning arts and lewd skills, who are forever wallowing in the haunts of fame and the thickets of profit (
lì sǒu

, the gathering place of wealth and gain), who are forever exacting over abacus, peck, and scales, who want both fame and profit and also to become immortals and Buddhas — that such as these should come and learn the Way, is it not laughable?

As for the word 'temper,' no one has it in balance. Who possesses firm resolve? Who nourishes upright spirit? Men merely let all their floating temper, irritable temper, hot-blooded temper, and vulgar temper show in their looks, or contend for victory in their words, or strive for mastery in their deeds, or play the hero in their anger, recognizing temper and not principle. How could they have the vast, flowing spirit? That such people also come to learn the Way — is it not laughable! For this root of illness, if you seek the method of cutting it off: the Confucians say, 'Unrighteous wealth and honor are to me as floating clouds'; and again, 'Hold fast your will; do not let your temper run wild.' The Buddhists say, 'Not receiving blessings, one accomplishes through patience.' The Daoists say, 'Break wholly with stinginess and greed; be compassionate and humble your temper.' All these can remove the root of the wealth-and-temper illness.

For these four things above, if you would cut off the root of illness, you must rectify your heart and thoughts. With the Confucians it lies in waking, with the Buddhists in awakening, with the Daoists in realizing. If you can wake, awaken, and realize, then you will see through all the affairs of the world."
When Master Chongyang had finished the principle of removing illness, Ma Danyang and Sun Bu'er asked again, "How is the work of sitting in meditation to be practiced?" Master Chongyang said:

In quiet sitting, forget emotion; stop thoughts, and when the mind dies the spirit lives. Spread a thick cushion, loosen your clothes and belt, and at the hour of the rat, facing east, sit cross-legged in meditation in gentle ease. Clench the fists firmly, straighten the body, click the teeth, swallow the saliva, touch the tongue to the palate, and listen with the ear turned inward. Open the eyes slightly and let the eyelids droop, turning the light of the spirit back to shine below the navel — this is called the mysterious gate.

In the work of quiet sitting, one must stop false thoughts. If there is the least false thought, the spirit is not pure yang, and the work is hard to accomplish. One must also forget emotion; if emotion is not forgotten, the mind is not at peace, and the Way too is hard to accomplish.

To spread a thick cushion is to make sitting endurable and the body untired. To loosen clothes and belt is to let the qi move and rest. The hour of the rat is the hour when the yang qi arises. Facing east is to take in the qi of life. Sitting cross-legged is to gather and nourish the spirit and qi. To clench the fists firmly means to make a fist with the two thumbs pressed on the third fingers, in order to forget the body. To straighten the body and spine is to let the two spaces be unobstructed, so that the qi is not blocked. Clicking lips and teeth together keeps the tower of many stories (another name for the throat) from wasting qi. The mouth is the opening of qi; when the mouth opens, the qi scatters, and so it should be kept closed. Turning the hearing inward: the ear connects with the aperture of essence and is given over to sounds, so one turns the hearing back and does not listen. Opening the eyes slightly keeps one from falling into darkness. The eye is the aperture of the spirit; the eye is harmed by forms, and the spirit scatters with forms. If the eyes are fully open the spirit is exposed; if fully closed the spirit is dark; hence the eyelids are half lowered. The light of the eye turns back from the mysterious palace to shine below the navel, just as the sun and moon in heaven give light and bring forth the ten thousand things. Few words gather the qi, so that the qi does not leak from the mouth; cutting off sounds nourishes the essence, so that the essence does not leak from the ear; emptying the marks of form stabilizes the spirit, so that the spirit does not leak from the eye. Therefore such a one is called a true man without outflows."

When Master Chongyang had finished expounding the Way, he added, "This is the work of sitting in meditation, the gate of entry to the Way. Do not regard it as vain; you should practice it diligently, and there will surely be results. Do not be slack, and so ruin your own future." Having spoken, the master gave further special guidance.

Ma Danyang and Sun Bu'er silently grasped his meaning. They took leave of the master and each returned to their own place, practicing according to the method, and by degrees there were results. They thought the Way ended here, and came no more to the hut to inquire into its subtleties, only doing this one practice to the full. More than a month passed. Ma Danyang was sitting in meditation in the side room when he saw Master Chongyang walk in. Ma Danyang rose to welcome him in. When the master was seated, he said to Danyang:

The Great Way is inexhaustible; draw on it and it is not drained, use it and it is not used up. You must let it penetrate the ten thousand transformations, and not cling to any one side. You must turn to the Way with a sincere heart and truly correct your faults; only then will it benefit body and mind. The Way is not attained unless you turn toward it; not for a moment or an instant may you depart from your original substance. Every word and every act must come from the inch-wide heart; keep clear and unclouded, and let every thought be benevolent — this is truly turning toward the Way. If a fault is not corrected, it is not removed. If the illness lies in selfishness, then with a public heart remove the selfishness; if the illness lies in desire, then with a principled heart remove the desire; if the illness lies in partiality, then with a centered heart remove the partiality; if the illness lies in pride, then with a harmonious heart remove the pride. Wherever the illness is, there treat the illness. Seeking help in this way, as soon as it arises you are aware of it; as soon as you are aware you sweep it away; as soon as you sweep it away it perishes. Then of itself the heart is harmonious as the spring wind, bright as the stars and moon, broad as heaven and earth, still as a mountain. Gradually the qi fills and the spirit overflows, silently moving the one origin, filling the four limbs, and before you know it, the Great Way is accomplished."

Let us leave aside Master Wang Chongyang's discourse on the Way with Ma Danyang, and speak again of Sun Bu'er, who was sitting alone in her room working at meditation. Suddenly she saw Master Wang Chongyang push aside the door curtain and walk into the room. Sun Bu'er was startled and rose hurriedly to her feet. Just as she was about to ask him a question, she saw the master smile and say, "The principle of the Way is subtle, the method of the Way is boundless; one body penetrates all, and ten thousand streams pay homage to the source. You must do it lively and quick, walk it naturally and freely — only then is there merit. Sitting here cold and clammy, lone and solitary as you do, is always without benefit. Do you not know that a lone yin does not generate and a solitary yang does not grow? Sitting dead like this, so that yin and yang cannot communicate, how can you conceive a fetus? How can you give birth to an infant? I tell you: if you want this, you cannot do without that; if you want that, still you cannot do without this."

With his talk of this and that, Master Wang Chongyang left Madam Sun crimson to the ears, overwhelmed with shame, and trembling all over with rage. She hurriedly pushed the door curtain aside, ran outside, and sat down in the front hall. Then she summoned the maidservant Qiu Xiang: "Go quickly and ask the squire to come." Seeing her mistress in such a rage, Qiu Xiang dared not delay, and hurried to the front side room to fetch Squire Ma. Danyang was keeping Master Chongyang company as he expounded the wondrous Way when suddenly he saw Qiu Xiang come in flustered and say to Squire Ma, "I do not know why the mistress is angry; she is sitting in the front hall and has sent me to fetch you, sir, saying she has something to say." Ma Danyang at once took leave of the master: "Please sit at ease a while, master; your disciple will be back directly." Master Chongyang nodded once and said, "Go, go." What came of this going? Read on.
Since she knew not the meaning of 'this' and 'that,' she raised a mind of such and such a kind.

blocks.text: 09. Wang Chongyang Divides His Body to Save Others; Sun Bu'er in Anger Confronts Her Master

inline.s: To save all beings I give the true transmission;
Of nothing and of something the mouth cannot tell; well I know the Great Way is not far off, yet without a focused mind a man loses his chance.

Now when Ma Danyang heard Qiu Xiang's words — that Madam Sun was in the hall, angry and unappeased, and wished to see the squire to say something — he said to the master, "It seems my companion Sun is troubled by something and wants me to go and talk with her. Please sit at ease a while, master; I shall go and return in a moment to keep you company." Master Wang Chongyang laughed and said, "Go, go." Ma Danyang left the front side room and came into the hall, where he saw Sun Bu'er, her face crimson, beside herself with anger. Ma Danyang put on a smiling face and asked her, "Why are you angry, companion Sun? Has some servant of the household offended you? As mistress you must be more generous and not stoop to quarrel with them." Sun Bu'er said, "Senior brother, you do not know. We took Wang Chongyang for a man of the Way, but who would have thought the old fellow utterly improper! Just now he came into my bedroom and said a great many things not fit to hear; it is truly infuriating. I will study this Way no longer." Ma Danyang asked, "When did the master come to your room?" Sun Bu'er said, "Just now." Ma Danyang said, "Then that is a lie. The master has been in my room expounding the Way since morning and has not stirred a step; nor have I left his side. The master is in my room now, and Qiu Xiang saw him when she came to fetch me. If you do not believe it, ask Qiu Xiang and you will know."

Before Sun Bu'er could speak, Qiu Xiang said, "When I went to fetch the master, old Mr. Wang was discoursing of heaven and earth with great relish. After the master came away with me, I do not know whether he is still there or not." Hearing this, Sun Bu'er bowed her head and said nothing. Ma Danyang, fearing the master had waited long in the side room, said no more to Sun Bu'er and hurried back to the side room.

Now Sun Bu'er, choking with a bellyful of anger, had hoped to call Ma Danyang out and give the master a good scolding to vent her spleen; but instead she was left feeling foolish, and in low spirits she too went back to the inner chambers.

Another month or more passed. Ma Danyang came in person to the thatched hut to ask the master about the Way. Master Chongyang said, "Sit down a while, and I will speak to you." Then he sighed deeply and said:

Alas! Those in the world who cultivate the Way — some cultivate in their deeds, some in their looks, some in their words — all miss it by far and have not a hair of the Way. Others cultivate through ear and eye, through belly and paunch, through reverence; but all methods of doing are not the Way. They lose the substance of the true Way, and cannot be called the Way.

The signs of this show themselves, and cannot be told in full. Some come near to heterodox paths; some make a pretense of cultivation; some are heavy with ostentation and short on calm; some have urgent aspiration but feeble strength. Each has its own illness: the illness here is that it is too light, the illness there that it is too heavy; none proceeds naturally from the center. Hence they rejoice in one thing and grieve over another, advance an inch and retreat a fathom, and never possess the wondrous savor of the Great Way — and in truth they do not know it.
In sum: if the human mind is not extinguished, the mind of the Way is not penetrated.

That the human mind is not extinguished means that worldly feelings are not seen as light. Clothing must not be unadorned; food and drink must not be unpalatable; reputation must not go unheralded; talent must not go unshown; silver and goods must not be few; fields and houses must not be small. In all things unable to see lightly, one has a heart that seeks blessings; now one has a wish for comfort, now a lament over poverty, now a thought of luxury. A bosom full of private desire — this is what is called the human mind.

That it is not diminished means one cannot see worldly things lightly and let them go. Every man possesses the true nature; it is a vessel of the Way that can be forged, a foundation that can be perfected. Yet because he cannot see worldly things lightly, the mind of the Way is not penetrated.

What is called the mind of the Way is this: to see being lightly, to see non-being lightly, to see beauty lightly, to see ugliness lightly, to see gain lightly, to see loss lightly, to see blame lightly, to see praise lightly, to see life lightly, to see death lightly. To be able to see all things lightly — this is the mind of the Way. Use this mind to cultivate the Way, and the Way can be accomplished; use it to subdue demons, and the demons vanish of themselves. Can one who cultivates the Way fail to remove the human mind and preserve the mind of the Way? May everyone but bring forth the mind of the Way and attain the fruit of true awakening."

Let us not speak of Master Chongyang's discourse on the Way with Ma Danyang, but tell again of Sun Bu'er, who, ever since the day she was left speechless in the hall by a few words from Ma Danyang, had gone back to her room unconvinced. If she said she had been dreaming, she had not slept — so where could the dream have come from? Besides, she had plainly seen him come in, and his words were still ringing in her ears; why then did they say he had been in the side room and never moved? No one could guess the reason. While she was still puzzling over it, she saw Master Wang Chongyang lift the curtain and come in with a grin, saying, "The Great Way makes no distinction between man and woman; apart from yin and yang the Way cannot be achieved." Sun Bu'er let him come in and sit down, while she herself withdrew and stood by the doorpost, and asked, "Master, why do you leave your meditation in the thatched hut and come to a woman's chamber?" Master Chongyang said, "Because you have turned your back on the furnace of creation, sitting alone in quiet meditation until your qi withers. A woman without a husband is a complaining woman; a man without a wife is a lonely man. I tell you plainly now: the one yin and the one yang must not be lacking. The pairing of yin and yang is the true principle; the yellow dame urges the cup and lifts the pot. The girl of the western house, the lad of the eastern house, each in harmony, well matched the two. Only because the old crone Yellow acts as go-between are husband and wife joined and enter the bridal chamber. When the two eights match, they return to mutual response and form a fetus at their side. When ten months of warming and nourishing are complete, an infant is born, stronger than other men. If you do as I say, you will straightway ascend to the heavenly palace and pay homage to the Jade Emperor." Hearing this, Sun Bu'er made no reply, but went out the door and, dragging the two door leaves shut, bolted them from the outside. Her one thought was to keep her earlier word and have it out face to face; she went to find Ma Danyang. Seeing the side-room door closed, she asked the household servant Ma Xing. Ma Xing said, "The squire has gone to the thatched hut." At these words Sun Bu'er set off for the thatched hut.

Now Ma Danyang was in the thatched hut keeping Master Wang Chongyang company as he expounded the Way. The master had just come to the point 'the human mind must be light, the mind of the Way must be true' when he suddenly burst out laughing and said to Danyang, "You had better go quickly! Someone has come looking for you." Hearing the master's words, Ma Danyang feared a visitor had arrived, so he took leave of the master, came out of the thatched hut, and walked toward the front hall. He ran head-on into Sun Bu'er, who seized his clothes with one hand and said, "Come and look." Ma Danyang asked, "Look at what?" Sun Bu'er said, "Do not ask; just come and look, and you will understand." Ma Danyang had no choice but to follow her all the way to the door of the inner chamber; Sun Bu'er pulled the fastening open and told him to go in and look. Ma Danyang, not knowing what it was about, had to go in. He looked around: the bed and bedding were as before, the boxes and trunks just as they had been, and apart from table and chairs there was nothing else. So he asked Sun Bu'er, "What did you call me in to see?" Sun Bu'er said, "To see your master!" Ma Danyang said, "The master is in the thatched hut expounding the Way to me — what master is there here?" Sun Bu'er did not believe him and came in herself, lifted the curtain, threw back the quilt, and searched everywhere under the bed and behind it, but found no trace at all, saying over and over, "How strange! How strange!" Ma Danyang said, "What is so strange? This is because your resolve for the Way is impure and you have been possessed by a demon." Sun Bu'er said, "What are you saying, senior brother! In all my life I have had no stray thoughts, and my one heart loves stillness. How could I be possessed? Twice the master came into my room; his face is vivid before my eyes, his voice still in my ears, his words clearly remembered. How could that be possession?" Ma Danyang said, "Tell me what words the master spoke." So Sun Bu'er repeated to Ma Danyang all the words Master Chongyang had spoken on his two visits to her room. Ma Danyang laughed aloud and said, "Companion Sun, clever all your life, foolish for a moment — this time you have been deluded." Sun Bu'er said, "How am I deluded?"
Ma Danyang said:

One who studies the Way must empty his heart and lower his tone, and not be ashamed to ask of those beneath him; only then does he gain one step and go on to the next, each step higher than the last. Thread by thread he gathers, and it becomes a foot; foot upon foot, and it becomes a yard; yard upon yard, and it becomes a fathom. Ten makes a hundred, a hundred makes a thousand, a thousand makes ten thousand. Yet the wonder of the Way is not reckoned by numbers, and so it is said that the wonder of the Way is without limit. You have now gained a little of the mysterious work, and you think the Way ends there. Every month you cling to this house of yours, sitting withered in ashen despondency, understanding neither the principle of yin and yang nor the workings of creation, and never going before your master to seek instruction. Held back by the difference between man and woman, you have raised up the view of self and other. When the master saw you dead-set in this method, unable ever to finish the Way, he wished to come in person and instruct you; but he too was hindered by the risk of scandal, and therefore his yang spirit appeared, dividing its body to save and convert you.

The master has told me again and again: 'One yin and one yang, that is called the Way; apart from yin and yang the Way cannot be completed.' This yin and yang is the yin and yang of the yang fire and the yin tally. It does not mean the yin and yang of men marrying and women taking husbands, of ordering the world. 'This' speaks of so wondrous a principle, and it is a pity you do not awaken to it. 'That' speaks of such a mystery, and I sigh that you do not know it. 'The lone yang does not grow': yang belongs to fire, and when fire is excessive it must grow feverish, and the elixir cannot be formed. 'The orphaned yin does not arise': yin gives birth to water, and when water is excessive it must overflow, and the elixir cannot be formed. This 'orphaned yin and lone yang' is a figure for water and fire that cannot aid each other.

In sum, one who cultivates the Way must have water and fire aiding each other and yin and yang running through, and only then can the elixir be returned. When he says you 'have turned your back on the furnace of creation,' he is plainly telling you that you do not understand the principle of true yin and true yang. 'The grown man and the complaining maiden' also means 'the orphaned yin does not arise, the lone yang does not grow.' So he plainly tells you that one who studies the Way cannot be without this yin and yang. This yin and yang is the wondrous function of returning the elixir. The 'yellow dame' is true intent. To join yin and yang through true intent is like lifting the jug and urging a man to drink fine wine (
liáng yùn

, good wine). True intent belongs to earth, and earth encloses yellow, and so she is figured as a dame. The maiden of the Western House is metal; metal flourishes in the west, and so she is called the Western House. The young man of the Eastern House is wood; wood flourishes in the east, and so it is said that 'east and west match each other.' 'Two and eight' is the number of one catty. Metal cannot be subdued unless it is the child of wood, and wood cannot be born unless it is the child of metal; this is the principle of yin and yang, creation, and the mutual overcoming of the five phases.

One who cultivates the Way must join them through intent, like a matchmaker reconciling two houses, so that metal and wood meet, with nothing between them, like the love of husband and wife. The 'bridal chamber' is the elixir court; it brings metal and wood home to the elixir court. 'Metal' is the corporeal soul; 'wood' is the ethereal soul. Gather these two souls in one place, clinging and unwilling to part, leaning one upon the other: the ethereal soul does not leave the corporeal soul, the corporeal soul does not leave the ethereal soul, like husband and wife, the two matching each other. Quicksilver is eight ounces, and lead is eight ounces as well. 'Mutual response' is where the elixir is formed. It means that the two souls lean upon each other; when essence and qi seem to respond, they congeal within, as in conception. 'Ten months' means the number is complete. 'Warm nourishment' is the firing times. This speaks of essence and qi congealing and being refined by the firing times into the elixir. 'Full' means perfect and complete: when the work is perfect and complete, the infant is born. The 'infant' is the spirit transformed from true qi. When this spirit comes forth from the Mud Pill Palace, ascends to pay court at the Golden Gate, and becomes a realized man, is that not to be an immortal?"
When Danyang had finished speaking, Bu'er was greatly awakened. If you would know what happened afterward, read the next chapter.
Yin and yang in harmony, true intent runs through; / bodhi's clear light, the mind's own traces, view;
Would you in the Pure Land seek the mystery through? / The Way lies with the master, the practice with you.

blocks.text: 10. Preaching the Three Vehicles, He Expounds the Way of Complete Truth; Ruining Her Countenance, She Gladly Becomes an Ugly Woman

inline.s: Once the true transmission is won, the Way may be plied; / the three vehicles' wondrous Dharma waits for you to decide.
That day Yuanzhen marred her own face, you recall, / to gain a golden body through ten thousand autumns' fall.

The story tells that when Sun Bu'er heard Ma Danyang's words they fell on her like a blow to the head, shattering the net of her delusion and bringing her to sudden awakening, as though she had started from a dream. She sighed and said, "Had it not been for your words, Elder Brother, I would nearly have ruined the great matter. Ordinarily I am a little quicker of understanding than you, Elder Brother; so why, once I took up the study of the Way, am I not your equal?" Ma Danyang said, "It is not that you are not my equal; it is only that you would not go and seek instruction, and so you are not my equal. Hence the saying, 'The clever are undone by their own cleverness; many a clever man has undone himself.' In the affairs of the world, only learning brings knowledge. How many are born knowing?" Sun Bu'er thanked him, saying, "I shall reverently obey the master's instruction, and from today I shall humbly seek teaching." Ma Danyang was greatly pleased, and went back to the side rooms by himself. Several days passed, and he had to go to his maternal uncle's house to offer birthday congratulations. He prepared all the gifts, explained the matter to the master, and invited Sun Bu'er to go with him. Sun Bu'er pleaded illness and would not go, so Ma Danyang had no choice but to order a servant boy to carry the gifts, and mounting his black donkey he set off for his uncle's house.

Leaving Danyang's journey aside, let us speak of Sun Bu'er in her room. Because Ma Danyang had said she would not seek instruction, and so did not understand the wonder of the Way, she took it to heart. Now, seeing that Ma Danyang was not at home and that all the servants, men and women, were at play in the front, she went alone to the thatched hut. Seeing the master sitting cross-legged in meditation, she knelt before him and said, "This disciple Sun Bu'er is dull of nature and does not understand the highest principle, and so has twice gone astray. Yesterday, thanks to Elder Brother's instruction, I learned that what you spoke before was the Way, and I repent it too late. I beg the master to pardon me and instruct me once more." So saying, she knocked her head several times without pause. Master Wang Chongyang said, "Stand up, and I will speak with you. The Way has three vehicles; one acts according to his measure. Now I will expound them for you, and we shall see which vehicle you can study." Then Sun Bu'er rose and stood to one side, bowing as she listened to the teaching.
Master Chongyang said:
One who studies the Way must set life and death beyond his concern; if he can break through this one word 'death,' he may become a man who does not die.

The highest vehicle is the Way of emptiness and nothingness. Not one thread hanging, not one speck of dust clinging, like the bright moon in an empty sky with not a cloud for ten thousand li. Only a single point of the spirit-root, and one can seize the creation of heaven and earth and fathom the true principle of yin and yang. Refine it by the method, and one can make the existent return to nothingness and from nothingness give birth again to the existent. One may grow old together with heaven and earth and cultivate as long as the sun and moon: this is the Way of the highest grade of celestial immortals.

The middle vehicle is to keep the precepts with reverent sincerity, to serve the sages and the true with worship, to recite the holy names of the Heavenly Worthy and to intone the secret writings of the Most High. When a single thought is pure and true, ten thousand cares are all made clear; one reaches up to the azure vault, and all spirits see into one, and the light of the spirit is not extinguished. A single point of true nature goes straight through to emptiness and nothingness, and one takes rank among the immortals: this is the Way of the middle vehicle.

As for the lowest vehicle, it is to pile up merit and accumulate practice. Widely practice skillful means, aid men and benefit beings; do many good deeds and constantly examine one's own faults. Then the true nature will not be darkened, and the spiritual brightness can of itself shine forth. Now hidden, now manifest, no different from an immortal: this is the Way of the lowest vehicle.
Weigh your own strength: which vehicle do you wish to study? I shall transmit to you the true method."
Sun Bu'er said, "This disciple wishes to study the highest vehicle, the Way of celestial immortals."

Master Chongyang laughed and said, "Your heart is large indeed, but I fear your resolve is not firm." Sun Bu'er said, "My heart is not large, but my resolve is very firm. This body can be destroyed, but my resolve cannot be taken from me." Master Chongyang said, "Whoever cultivates the Way must obtain the spiritual power of mountains and rivers, and so the lay of the land must be chosen. Now in Luoyang of the Eastern Commandery the spiritual power is at its height, and a true immortal ought to appear there. If you go to that place and cultivate for twelve years, you may hope to accomplish the Way. Can you go?" Sun Bu'er said, "This disciple is willing to go."

Master Chongyang looked at her once, shook his head, and said, "You cannot go! You cannot go!" Sun Bu'er said, "This disciple would cast aside life and forget death; why can I not go?" Master Chongyang said, "If one dies, one must die to some purpose. If you die to no purpose, have you not thrown your life away for nothing? Luoyang is a thousand li from here, and along the road there are many gallants and wandering blades, and very many frivolous young men. If they see that your face is like a flower and your looks like jade, how would their hearts not be stirred? At the least they will speak wild words in jest, and at the worst they will surely offer you insult. Yours is a nature of chastity and ardor; how could you bear their foul defilement? You would certainly stake your life to preserve your name and honor. You meant to seek long life, and would instead lose your life. That is why I say you cannot go."

When Sun Bu'er heard this she pondered for a long while. Without taking leave of the master, she left the thatched hut and went to the kitchen, where she sent away everyone who did the cooking. With her own hands she lit the fire and poured a whole jar of clear oil into the pan. When the oil was boiling, she took a bowl of cold water in her hand, turned her face toward the pan, shut both eyes tight, steeled her heart, and poured the cold water into the pan. The boiling oil, meeting the cold water as it burst in, spattered oil drops all over her face, and everywhere the drops fell they were scalded into blisters. Enduring the pain, Sun Bu'er came to see the master and said, "In this state, master, may I go?" At the sight of her Master Chongyang clapped his hands and laughed, saying, "Wonderful! Wonderful! That the world should hold a person of such great resolve; my journey to Shandong was not made in vain." Having spoken, the master at once transmitted to Sun Bu'er the whole of the wondrous principle of yin and yang, the mysterious workings of creation, and the work of refining yin into yang and transcending the ordinary to enter sagehood.

When the transmission was done, he said, "The great Way is hidden in not knowing and not recognizing. This work of not knowing and not recognizing must wait upon a touch of madness before it can be concealed from others, so that they do not know that I have this work, nor recognize that I am practicing. Only on the day the great work is accomplished may one appear in person to preach the Dharma. Wait until the oil blisters on your face have healed, then go quickly to Luoyang. There is no need to come and take leave of me; when your merit is round and your fruit is full, we shall meet again at the Peach Banquet."

When the master had finished speaking, he closed his eyes and said no more. Sun Bu'er bowed to the master several times and left the thatched hut. She saw the serving women and maids come in from outside, and meeting her head-on they were startled out of their wits. Had she not worn her usual clothes, they would scarcely have known her. They all came at once to ask, "What is the reason for this?" Sun Bu'er said, "I wanted to make a few fried cakes for old Mr. Chongyang, and feared that you were not clean, so I sent you all away. Working with my own hands, I carelessly poured cold water into the boiling oil, and could not dodge in time, and so my whole face was scalded into blisters. This is a passing calamity of mine, nothing very serious; you need not be alarmed. Go about your proper business, each of you, and do not let me be on your minds." Having spoken, she went back to her inner room, shut the door, and silently took up the work the master had transmitted, doing it one item at a time. The oral instructions and wondrous words she rehearsed anew.

Two days later Danyang returned. As he was about to enter the gate, the serving women told him that Sun Bu'er's face had been scalded by boiling oil. Ma Danyang sighed without end. He first went to the thatched hut and paid his respects to the master, then came to the main chamber to see Sun Bu'er. He saw that her whole face was covered with blisters, and that the blisters had already festered and burst, with yellow fluid running in streams, turning a face like a flower and jade into the visage of a ghost. At the sight Ma Danyang could not but groan, and he called out, "Fellow cultivator Sun, why were you not careful, that the oil scalded you into this state? How you have suffered!"

Before he had finished speaking, Sun Bu'er opened her eyes wide, looked at Ma Danyang, and laughed without stopping. She stepped forward, seized Ma Danyang with one hand, and said, "Are you a boy of the Queen Mother of the West? She has sent you to invite me to the Peach Banquet; today I shall go with you to the heavenly palace. Hurry! Hurry!" So saying, she climbed up on the table, clutched at the window lattice with her hands, and made as if to rise into the air. Suddenly she fell with a thump, lay on the ground, and moaned without ceasing.

Ma Danyang hastily helped her up, but she wept and laughed by turns. Seeing her in such a state, Ma Danyang felt a certain desolation in his heart, and went again to the thatched hut to see the master, saying, "My fellow cultivator Sun has gone mad with longing for immortality; what is to be done?" Master Chongyang said, "If one is not mad and not addled, who would become an immortal?" When Ma Danyang would have questioned him further, the master had already closed his eyes and entered stillness, and paid him no heed at all. Seeing that the master would not answer, Ma Danyang had no choice but to leave the thatched hut and return to the front hall, dejected and joyless.

Let us tell again how Sun Bu'er, with a few mad words, sent Danyang away, and so won quiet and stillness for herself, exactly right for the work. She worked until her nature-substance was round and bright, a wonder beyond words. When her mind ground grew clear, she first understood how many benefits there are in pursuing the Way, and was exceedingly glad. She took up a mottled-bronze mirror and looked at herself, and was startled. She saw her whole face scarred, red and black in patches, and having gone more than a month without combing her hair or dressing, her hair was a tangled mass, like a shaggy-haired ghoul; in truth a Kumbhanda, a living yaksha. In no way did she look like a squire's wife. When Sun Bu'er had studied her own appearance, she was overjoyed within, and said to herself that now she could go to Luoyang.

So she tore her clothes into tatters at random, smeared a handful of soot from the pan over her face, ran out before the hall, and laughed three times aloud. At once she startled all those maids and serving girls, the household servants and the young lads, who all came together and surrounded her. When Sun Bu'er saw them press close, she made to go out. The maids came to pull her back, and Sun Bu'er bit about her with her mouth. There was one maid who was closest to her; she clutched at Sun Bu'er's clothes and would not let go, and Sun Bu'er turned her head and bit her hand so hard that it bled. The maid let go her hand, and Sun Bu'er was already gone. The serving women and maids, seeing how fierce she was, dared not pull her back, and hurried to report it to the squire. Now it is told that Ma Danyang was sitting in meditation in the side room when he suddenly heard a clamor outside. He rose quickly from his seat and came out to look, and saw the servants come and report, "Madam Sun has gone violently mad and has run out of the house." When Ma Danyang heard this, he feared some mishap, and urgently ordered the servants to give chase at once, while he himself came after them.

Now Sun Bu'er walked straight out of the estate, and the men who kept the gate could not stop her. The people before and behind the estate did not recognize her at once as Madam Sun, and so she got away. Sun Bu'er knew that someone would surely come after her. Seeing a heap of wild brush beyond the village, she plunged into it. Sure enough, Ma Danyang came up with the servants and lads, the women and maids, all in pursuit; they went on ahead for a while, then suddenly turned back and went off again by the way they had come.

Sun Bu'er saw it all clearly from the brush, and only when they had gone far did she come out and set off toward the southwest. By day she begged in the villages, by night she lodged in old temples, always in desolate, secluded, uninhabited places: great trees, sheer cliffs, any spot that could keep off the rain. If anyone came to ask her questions, she gave one line about heaven and one about earth, raving and babbling, weeping and laughing. Seeing her in this state, people knew she was a madwoman and asked her no more. And so all along the road she went safe and sound, and when she met men of upright conduct she would ask the way. In less than two months she reached Luoyang. Whether she truly could accomplish the Way and become an immortal, read the next chapter to learn.
A single leaf of a boat roams the great sea; / the ten-thousand-fathom waves bring no alarm to me.

blocks.text: 11. Hail Falls, and Heaven's Lord Protects the Dharma; Wondrous Reckoning Is Cast, and the Realized Man Points Out the Way

inline.s: Long years mired and sunk in the drowning tide, / where the river of craving rolls, its billows sky-wide;
Cultivate, and you may climb the farther shore; / why seek another boat in midstream any more?

The story tells that after Sun Bu'er left Ma Family Estate she feigned madness all along the road. She traveled several months and came to the outskirts of Luoyang, where there was a broken tile kiln, and there she took shelter. She often went into the county town to beg for food, playing the madwoman to the utmost. She set the little children trailing after her in a pack, crying, "There goes the madwoman, long and short!" and so they made her name known. Inside and outside the town and countryside everyone knew her for a madwoman, and no one came to trouble her any more. Thus she could set her mind at ease and awaken to the Way, which matched Master Chongyang's words, "The great Way is hidden in madness."

It is further told that in Luoyang county there were two notorious ruffians, one named Zhang San and one named Li Si, who were forever lewd and swindling and stopped at nothing. They had often seen Sun Bu'er begging in the streets; ugly as her face was, her eyes were bright and her teeth white, and but for the many scars on her face her looks would not have been poor. These two ruffians took note of her with their eyes and laid it up in their hearts. That night the moon was white and the breeze clear, the sky full of stars, and the two were coming back from the countryside, where they had cheated honest folk. Mellow with drink, they came to a place not far from the broken tile kiln, and Zhang San said, "Let us go and amuse ourselves with that madwoman!" Li Si said, "Do not go, do not go. I have heard tell that if a man lies with a madwoman he is unlucky all his life and never has any long run of fortune." Zhang San said, "We are men whom the gods of heaven will not take in and the gods of earth will not want; what do we care for a long run of fortune or no?" So he would not listen to Li Si, and went on straight toward the broken tile kiln, and Li Si had no choice but to follow him on ahead. They had not gone many steps when suddenly they saw a black cloud overhead, close by the kiln, and with a sudden crack of thunder, as if the mountains were falling and the earth splitting, it burst above their heads and shook Zhang San and Li Si until they trembled in every limb.

That black cloud scattered in an instant, and heaven and earth went dark, so that a man could not see his own hand. A wild wind sprang up and blew through the two of them until the cold pierced their bones. Then a fierce rain came down, drumming on their heads like a war drum, until their heads swam and ached. Li Si put up his hand to shield his skull, and the rain struck the back of his hand like iron pellets, and only then did he know it was not rain; it was hail, which men call snow-pellets, and in common speech cold ones. The cold ones beat the two of them until they had nowhere to turn and no place to hide. Li Si said without ceasing, "A living retribution! I said we should not come, and you would come by force; now let us see how it goes." When Zhang San heard Li Si reproaching him, he grew angry, and all at once his foot came down on a hailstone. The hailstone was smooth and slippery, and how could a foot stand firm on it? He slid and fell flat, scrambled up in a flurry, and stepped once more on empty air and fell flat again, as though someone were pushing him. He stumbled again and again, until his head was cut and his eyes swollen, his flesh mangled and his blood running, and he could only cry out to heaven.

Before long the clouds parted and the moon appeared, and the sky was full of stars again. Li Si had taken a few cold ones, but he never stumbled or fell, and so came to no great harm; only Zhang San, after those falls, was dizzy and dim-sighted, and could only put out his tongue, shake his head, and say, "This will never do! This will never do! That madwoman is not to be trifled with!" Li Si said, "Only now do you know she is not to be trifled with; let us see whether you will come again next time!" Talking as they went, the two made their way home. Li Si told the whole story to those vagabonds and ruffians; one man told ten, and ten told a hundred, and so those who would not learn to be good, and the beggars too, never dared come to the broken tile kiln again. Sun Bu'er stayed in Luoyang twelve years, cultivating and awakening to the Way, and never once did a wicked man trouble her; all of it was thanks to Li Si. Later readers, coming to this place in the book, have a poem that sighs:
Here the realized man awakened to the mysterious work; / how could a mad ruffian come to play the bravo's part?
When the hail came down and he took his beating sore, / he learned that Heaven's Lord protects the Dharma evermore.

Master Wang Chongyang had been in Squire Ma's house more than a year without his noticing it. Out in the village a few old men were idly talking, and said, "Squire Ma does not know how to enjoy his good fortune. He has simply given away a whole family estate to an outsider, and driven his wife out of her wits; no one knows where she has gone." Among them was a man of fifty-odd years named Duan Anren, who said:

Yesterday I went to his estate to visit Squire Ma. There was no one keeping watch at the gate. When I went in, I did not see a single woman; there were only men. I asked where the squire was, and they told me, 'He is behind, in the thatched hut, listening to Master Chongyang preach the Way.' So I walked on back, and saw many thatched huts built there, with Squire Ma and Wang Chongyang sitting in meditation in the one in the middle. When Squire Ma saw me he came out at once and accompanied me to the front hall to talk. I asked him where his wife had gone, and Squire Ma said, 'She has her Way, and I have my wonder.' I asked again, 'Why do I not see the maids and serving girls?' The squire said, 'The men I have married off, the women I have married out; each has set up a household of his own, and there is no tie left to fret over.' I asked again, 'What are these thatched huts built for?' The squire said, 'To gather those who cultivate the Way, that they may awaken to the Way and nourish the true nature.' I asked again, 'Why does Master Chongyang never come out?' The squire said, 'He loves quiet above all things, and does not mix with worldly folk.' When I had asked my questions, I took leave of the squire and came away.

I met Ma Xing, and I put my questions to him as well. 'This estate of yours was so lively before; why is it so cold and still now, like a monastery?' Ma Xing said, 'You do not know. This Master Chongyang who has come to our house is a living immortal. He does not care for bustle; what he loves is quiet. Since Madam Sun left, he has sent away all the maids and serving women and menservants in the estate, and kept only a few of us old faithful ones to watch over the place; that is why it is so still.' I asked Ma Xing again, how he knew that Master Chongyang was a living immortal. Ma Xing answered me, 'In all the affairs of the household, and all that happened in former days, there is nothing anyone has to tell him; he knows it all. Is that not strange? And there are things still to come, and which day will be fair and which day rainy; there is nothing he does not know. Is he not a living immortal?'"

When Duan Anren had finished all he had to say about Ma Family Estate, one of the village elders, an old man of the Pan family, said, "By what you say, he knows things past and things to come. We have had this drought a long while and no rain has fallen; why do we not all go and ask him when the rain will come?" The village elders said with one voice, "Good!" So they came with Old Pan to Ma Family Estate. First they saw Squire Ma and explained their errand, and Ma Danyang led the elders to the thatched hut to ask Master Chongyang, "When will it rain?" The master said, "On the wall of the Earth God's shrine at the east end of your village, the date of the rain is written; go and look, and you will know." When the village elders heard this they came out of the estate at once, went back to their own village, and made their way to the east end. Arriving before the Earth God's shrine, they indeed saw several lines of writing on the whitewashed wall.

Old Pan read it out to the company: "Before the King of Men a pair of melons stands; a pearl shines upon the King's own lands; on the twenty-third day the heavy rain descends; from the monk's mouth mud comes forth from his hands." Below, in small characters, were written the words "Four Characters Unriddled." When Old Pan had read it he laughed and said, "This is a character riddle some schoolboy wrote here; what has it to do with the date of rain?" The village elders asked, "What character riddle is it? Can you guess it?" Old Pan said, "I am used to character riddles. How could I not guess it?" The village elders said, "Since you can guess it, guess it quickly and let us hear." Old Pan said, "Add a few drops of rain to the King of Men and you have the character for gold. Add one dot beside the character for king and you have the character for jade. 'On the twenty-third day the heavy rain descends' - fit the pieces together (join and gather them into one) and you have the character for full. From the monk take away the character for 'monk' and keep 'shang.' Mud is earth. Put 'shang' on top of earth - is that not the character for hall? Plainly it is the four characters 'gold and jade fill the hall.' Where is any date for rain in that?"

Duan Anren stepped forward, pointed with his finger at the line "on the twenty-third day the heavy rain descends," and said, "This is plainly the date of the rain, and you insist there is none. Though these are but a few dumb riddles, there is a hidden juncture in them. Today is the nineteenth; from the twenty-third it is only four days. Let us see whether there is rain on the twenty-third, and then we shall know whether he is efficacious or not." The village elders all said, "What you say is reasonable." So they went home, each to his own house. When the twenty-third day came, black clouds filled the sky and the rain poured down in torrents, from morning until noon, and only then did it stop. Only then did the villagers believe that Master Chongyang was a spirit.

There was also a man of the northern village who lost a cow; he searched everywhere and could not find it, and came to ask the master. Master Chongyang said, "The cow is in the southern village, up in a great tree, in a magpie's nest." When the man who had lost the cow heard this he could not help laughing, and said, "A cow that size, and a magpie's nest that tiny, how could it fit?" Master Chongyang said, "Go, and you will get your cow; say no more." The man had no choice but to leave the thatched hut and come to the southern village, where indeed he saw a very tall tree with a magpie's nest in it. Country folk know how to climb trees, so he climbed up to take the nest, and found it an empty one. He pulled at it with his hand, and a dead branch fell and struck him in the face. As he bowed his head a little, he saw a cow tethered inside a broken house in the village. Looking closely, it was the very cow he had lost. The cow was lying in the broken house with firewood and straw piled outside it and covered over on every side; had he not looked down from a height, he could never have seen it. The man hurried down from the tree, understanding in his heart that there had long been a gentleman on the roof in that village who was used to such work. Had the master not pointed the way, by nightfall the thief would have led the cow far off and sold it to someone else, and it could never have been found again. The man went into the broken house and led his cow home.

Of this we say no more. That day several people from the western village came with questions of their own. Among them was a boy of thirteen or fourteen, who said that his elder brother had been gone from home several months and he did not know when he would return, and so he had come to ask old Master Chongyang. Chongyang said, "Go home and ask your mother's hand." When the boy heard this he laughed without stopping. A little later he came home and saw his mother holding a letter in her hand, and she said, "Your elder brother is in business in Laizhou and has sent a letter back. The man who brought it has just gone; open the letter and read it to me." The boy opened the letter and read: "From your unworthy son, a letter offered to my kind mother. Since father's passing, I have been raised to manhood by your care. Now I carry out my father's purpose and engage in trade abroad, and things have gone fairly well. At present my accounts are not all collected, and I cannot return quickly to comfort my mother's heart. When the autumn cools, I shall come home in the middle of the ninth month to attend upon you with sweet dainties (fine foods)." The boy had not finished reading when he clapped his hands and laughed aloud, saying, "How efficacious! How efficacious!" His mother was just about to question him when she saw five or six men come to the gate; what they wanted, read the next chapter to learn.
But for the fisherman to lead the way, / how could one ever meet the waves?

blocks.text: 12. Pointing Out the Sitting Work, He Sets Forth the Wondrous Principle; Studying the True Way, He Joyfully Meets an Enlightened Master

inline.s: Love and kindness bind and tangle, past all untying; / when the day comes to go, none goes with you in your dying.
Now let your hands fall free, with nothing clinging fast, / and mount straight to the Jade Pool's white jade stair at last.

The story tells that the boy of the western village was just about to tell his mother what Master Chongyang had said about asking her hand, when suddenly he saw five or six men come to the gate and ask which road led to Ma Family Estate.
