The boy said, "You ask the way to Ma Family Estate; are you by chance going to see the living immortal?" Those men answered, "Just so." When the boy heard that they meant to see the living immortal, he was beside himself with delight, and said to them, "It is not far, not far; I will lead you there." So saying, he went on ahead. The company followed him out of the western village, and before long they came to Ma Family Estate. It was fated that they should have the affinity, for they happened to find Squire Ma sitting before the hall. Seeing them come in, he rose and welcomed them into the hall to be seated, and asked, "What brings you gentlemen to my humble estate?" The several men said, "We have come to seek the Way." When Ma Danyang heard this, he led them to the thatched hut to pay their respects to the master.

Among them was one surnamed Tan, named Chuduan, whose style was Changzhenzi. In former years he had been afflicted with a grave illness, and when Wang Chongyang first came to Shandong he had taught him the work of driving off sickness. Once well, he had set his whole mind on awakening to the Way, and had sought the master everywhere without finding a trace of him. Now he heard men say that a living immortal named Wang Chongyang had appeared at Ma Family Estate, and so he knew the master was here. He had also brought along a fellow seeker of the Way, surnamed Hao, named Datong, whose style was Taigu, a man of Wending county in this same prefecture. The other men too were seekers of the good; there is no need to record their names.

At once Tan Changzhen thanked the master for the kindness of his former healing, and then spoke of his wish to study the Way today. Master Chongyang said, "The Dharma-gate stands wide open: those who go, go; those who come, come; I hold back none who leave, and refuse none who come." He at once ordered Ma Danyang to send them to the second thatched hut to lodge. Some days later two more cultivators arrived: one surnamed Liu, named Chuxuan, whose style was Changshengzi, and one surnamed Wang, named Chuyi, whose style was Yuyangzi, both men of Shandong. Ma Danyang received them, asked their purpose, and found that they too had come to seek the Way, so he led the two of them to the thatched hut to pay their respects to the master. Master Chongyang ordered Ma Danyang to settle them in the third thatched hut. And so one came from the east and one from the west, and in less than a month several dozen had come. Master Chongyang had Ma Danyang agree with them on duties, each to manage one matter, with rules for all, and none might overstep his bounds (overstep his office without leave). When everything was settled, Master Chongyang discoursed with them on the sitting work. The disciples ranged themselves in two rows, bowed, and listened to the teaching.

Man's life has qi for its root, breath for its leader, the heart for its foundation, and the kidneys for its stem. Heaven and earth are eighty-four thousand li apart, and in man the heart and kidneys are eight inches and four tenths apart. The kidneys are the inner kidneys, three inches and three tenths below the navel. A single vessel runs straight through them, to give passage to the breath. The breath governs the hundred vessels: with one exhalation the hundred vessels all open, with one inhalation the hundred vessels all close. The creation of heaven and earth in its ceaseless movement is nothing other than these two words, exhalation and inhalation. If a man's breathing stays always between heart and kidneys, then the blood and qi will of themselves be smooth, the original qi will of itself be firm, the seven emotions will not blaze up, and the hundred illnesses will vanish without being treated.

As for the method of sitting meditation, at each of the hours zi, wu, mao, and you, spread a thick sitting mat in a quiet room. Sit cross-legged on the mat, with the eyes slightly open and looking toward the navel. Stop the ears with cotton, and let the mind cut off all thoughts and cares. Let the intent follow the breath, going and coming, rising and falling with the breath, neither too slow nor too fast, letting it be natural. After sitting the time of one stick of incense, you will find the breath at mouth and nose no longer coarse, but gradually soft and fine. After another stick of incense, you will find the breath at mouth and nose as though present and as though not. Then slowly stretch out the legs and open the eyes, take out the earplugs, and leave the seat to walk a few steps. Then lie down on your side for a while, and when you rise, sip half a bowl of congee broth. You must not do heavy work, and above all must not give way to anger, lest it spoil your work and injure the true qi."
The work of sitting is not in how much you sit; / it all depends on refining qi and putting demons to flight;
So sweep all hindrances away in one clean cast, / and let no net of snares about your heart be cast.
If hindrances are not cleared, the afflictions gather fast; / if the net is not untied, how can one roam at leisure at last?
The highest principle is plainly handed down to you: / do not by dawdling make your own road rough and rue.
[Putting demons to flight] To rid oneself of delusive thoughts. [Roam at leisure] Leisurely and carefree.
[Dawdling] To drag and be slack.

When Master Chongyang had finished discoursing on the sitting work, he left the seat to rest, and the disciples each returned to their quarters; of this we say no more. It is further told that in Dou village of Qixia county in the prefecture of Dengzhou, Shandong, there was a man surnamed Qiu, named Chuji, whose courtesy name was Qifa. There were three brothers: the eldest was Qiming, the second Qixing, and their parents had died early. This Qiu Qifa, thanks to the care of his elder brothers and their wives, grew to manhood. He had studied a few years and could also compose poems, lyrics, songs, and rhapsodies. But he had no heart for fame and rank; his whole bent was toward quiet, and he would often sit alone the whole day through, speaking to no one. It seemed that in this he found something to his liking, yet no one knew why it was so. His brothers and their wives urged him again and again to study and seek fame, and he answered them, "Study is for the fathoming of principle; why should I covet fame?" When they wished to arrange a marriage for him, he firmly refused, saying, "Before a man is established, how can he let marriage bind and hobble him (
xiè bàn

, entangle and bind)?" His brothers and their wives, hearing his words were out of the common, did not dare press him hard, and let him have his way. Qiu Qifa would often say to people, "A man lives in the world: if he does not seek a path by which to get out, but all day contends for fame and covets profit, is greedy for wife and clingingly fond of children, then when impermanence comes, all things are empty. Other men think the affairs of the world are all real; in my eyes they are drifting clouds and morning dew, a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow."

One day he heard men say that at Ma Family Estate in Ninghai county there was a Master Wang Chongyang, a man of wide virtue and a great cultivator, and that several men from Qixia county were studying the Way there. Qiu Qifa had loved the Way all his life, and when he heard this he too wished to go and study it. He had not yet made it known to his brothers and their wives, and he feared they would not let him go, so he had no choice but to quietly put together a little traveling money, take a few changes of clothes, and slip away secretly from home, heading for Ninghai county.

Before many days he reached Ma Family Estate. That day it happened that Ma Danyang was on duty; he asked his purpose, and wrote his name in the register. Tan, Liu, Wang, Hao, and the rest all came to look him over, and said with one voice, glad at heart, "So young a man, and he can sincerely study the Way; truly this is rarely heard of." So saying, they led him to the thatched hut to pay his respects to Master Chongyang. Ma Danyang then told the master of his wish to study the Way. Master Chongyang looked him over, shook his head, and said, "This man has too many thoughts and is too clever; he cannot study the Way. Let him hurry home at once and not ruin himself." Qiu Qifa knelt and said, "This humble one has set his whole heart on the Way, with no second thought; I beg the master to take me in." Ma Danyang too pleaded on his behalf, but the master would not consent, saying, "It is not that I will not take him; this man's root of suffering is very heavy, and I fear that later he will not endure the trials, and will surely conceive the thought of retreat and regret. Better not to take him at all." Qiu Qifa would have pleaded again, but Master Chongyang had gone out of the thatched hut to look at the flowers.

Ma Danyang and the others, having no recourse, could only lead Qiu Qifa to the front hall to lodge, set him to sweeping the hall, and privately passed on to him some breath-sitting practice. One day Qifa said to Ma Danyang, "Since the old master will not take me in, why should I not now take you as my teacher?" Ma Danyang said, "Not so, not so! When you seek a man you must seek a great man; when you take a teacher you must take a bright teacher. I but know a little of the elementary work; as for the great Way, I have not heard it either. Settle down and lodge here, and I will slowly manage things for you." Qiu Qifa, hearing this, was much pleased, and morning and evening served everything with diligence; whatever he was bidden, one call and one answer. After a few days he had grown acquainted with everyone, and each one liked him. One day he followed the elder Dharma-brothers to the thatched hut and saw Master Chongyang seated in the center, with the disciples standing on either side, listening in reverence to the teaching.

Since I have come here, I have held a grandmotherly heart and a bitter tongue to rescue the world and transform people, wishing to make everyone return to the path of awakening and, wherever they be, together quit the ford of confusion. Now I too am a man; born loving the Way, foolish and dull in youth, strange and odd in manhood, and divine in strength — the world that finds me marvelous all take me to be extraordinary!

Would I, then, be willing to be extraordinary? I am but dull, but ordinary, but stupid! Wherein am I strange? Not to prize wealth, not to envy, not to scheme, not to be false — that is my dullness. Not to know calculation, not to tell artful from clumsy — that is my stupidity. Not to speak of the strange, not to sink into the vulgar — that is my ordinariness.

The world says I am dull, laughs at my stupidity, and blames my ordinariness; but I on the contrary grieve that the world is dull to the utmost, stupid to the utmost, and ordinary to the utmost, yet does not know how to rouse itself. I therefore take the very way of the utmost dullness, stupidity, and ordinariness to awaken the world. If you cannot know this, then you do not know the Way. Hence the one who cultivates the Way must begin with tempering the mind.

Yet to temper before it arises is good, but the more precious is to temper after it has arisen. Such as the roaming mind, the released mind, and all the sundry-thoughted minds are minds that have already arisen. To make them still and unmoved, one must guard the mind, settle the mind, and gather the mind.

Now to guard the mind is to guard it when it has not yet stirred; to settle the mind is to settle it when it is about to stir; to gather the mind is to gather it when it has already stirred. To gather is not easy: first one must gather it as it arises. The swifter the gathering, the firmer the guarding; the firmer the guarding, the more enduring the settling — this is the wonder of our Way's mind-cultivation!

You must make this mind empty, without a single object. For the mind is formed by the true yang of the one qi of the original heaven. Hence the mind belongs to fire; it is not pure yang without yin, for within yang there is itself true yin. Therefore the shape of the heart-character has three dots covering above and a crescent moon bearing below. Thus we see that yang cannot grow without yin, and yin cannot be born without yang; true yin follows true yang, and so it is named the mind. Wherefore, at the slightest stir of a false thought, within the mind there is a fraction less of true qi. When a single matter enters the mind, there is added a kind of demonic obstruction. Hence once the mind stirs it is no longer called the mind but is named a thought. In the form of the thought-character, a man has two minds. When a man has two minds he cannot be single-minded; hence no undertaking succeeds, and he is all the farther from the Way!

Master Chongyang continued, "The mind is the master of the whole body; it is one, never two. If a second mind arises, that is what is called a thought. The instant this thought sprouts it gives birth to many vain and false affairs, and the mind can no longer be the master, so that this body sinks into drowning. Alas! it is hard to lift it out."

In the very midst of the discourse, Qiu Qifa, listening happily amid the crowd, kept crying out in praise! The master gave him a glare and then stopped speaking. When the disciples came out they all blamed him for making a noise, which had made the master stop. Qiu Qifa pretended not to hear, and let them grumble as they would. He reflected secretly that the master's words on tempering the mind were the very secret of cultivating the Way; and the one who cultivates the Way, if he does not first tune his mind well, even with the wondrous Way cannot succeed. So each day he reviewed his own mind, watching whether it erred, whether it was at fault. One day, seeing the elder Dharma-brothers were not in the front hall, he reasoned they must be listening to the master's discourse behind; so he too ran to listen. What did he hear? Listen to the next part for the answer.

blocks.text: 13. Disbanding the Altar, the Students Return Home; Exchanging for Taoist Robes, Master and Disciples Come South

inline.s: I grieve that worldlings grasp not the true void; / In flowers and wine their valor is employed;
The spring night's joy is brief, the long years roll; / And death's dread limit bears upon the soul;
Their cunning is as the cat that hunts the mouse, / While time, like the arrow from the bow, is loose;
They do not know how all their spirit is spent, / And would but lay this body in the earth’s content.

Now Qiu Qifa, seeing the elder Dharma-brothers and friends were not in the front hall, was sure they must be behind listening to the master's discourse. He straightway came to the thatched hut and indeed saw the master seated on the dais expounding the Dharma, with the disciples standing in order on either side. He did not go in, but stood outside the door to listen with a washed ear. He heard the master say:

In cultivating the thought, there is fineness within fineness. At one private thought there is a hair's worth of dregs in the mind; at one thought of desire there is thereupon a great demonic obstruction in the heart. For when private desire arises, the original heaven is lost. Only by removing private desire can the original heaven be kept.

The original heaven is the one qi. When private desire arises, fire moves; when fire moves, the qi is scattered; once the qi is scattered, what original heaven remains? And how then to watch the measure of the fire? When the private is heavy, the qi is worn out; how then restore the spirit's movement? When desire is excessive, the qi is dried up; how then gain the profound mystery? Its working is like this — should private thoughts be removed or not? Should desirous thoughts be removed or not? Should false thoughts be removed or not?

You who have private thoughts, hear my words and take heed! You who have desirous thoughts, take heed! You who have false thoughts, take heed! In all, you must nourish the mind into stillness without movement; then the thoughts can be extinguished. When thoughts are extinguished the private is exhausted; when the private is exhausted, desire is purified; when desire is purified, yang is pure; when yang is pure, yin vanishes. True immortals and great Buddhas all attain it from this, and all set to work at the place of thoughts. Do not regard it as idle talk (an empty theory divorced from actuality).

Master Chongyang was expounding the very subtlety when Qiu Qifa, forgetting himself in listening, cried out unthinkingly, "Good!" Master Chongyang said to the disciples, "The Dharma is spoken within the gate; a man outside listens. Let me ask, of all these, who is the one that knows the tone?" When the master had said this, Ma Danyang looked out, saw it was Qiu Qifa, and called him in.

At the sight of him the master turned angrily to Ma Danyang, "I instructed you to send him away; why is he still here?" Before he had finished, Liu Changsheng, Hao Taigu, Wang Yuyang, and Tan Changzhen together came forward and pleaded, "Since Qiu Qifa has come to take a teacher and seek the Way, we beg the master to take pity and gather him in, that morning and evening he may receive instruction." Master Chongyang said, "It is not that I will not take him, but I fear his heart is not genuine. When he once meets hardship he will conceive a mind to repent and turn back. Then the Way will not be cultivated, and he will instead incur sin; better that I not take him." Liu Changsheng and the others pleaded again and again, and Qiu Qifa knelt on the ground and would not rise. Master Chongyang said, "Since you have repeatedly recommended him, how can I refuse your good will? Such as you look after him, I shall take him now and give him the Taoist name Changchun." Qiu Qifa at once arose, performed the three kneelings and nine prostrations, bowed before the master, and then made his salute to the company. The master descended from his seat, and each returned to his place.

After another month or so, the master directed Ma Danyang to invite all the fellow practitioners together to the inner hall. For this discourse, an altar must be set up outside the hermitage. Ma Danyang took the master's word and saw it done at once. Before long the congregation had gathered, in trim dress and stately bearing, and together they came before the hermitage and asked the master to take the high seat and speak. Master Chongyang came out of the thatched hut, mounted the seat, composed his countenance, and sat upright; after a long while he said:

My teaching makes stillness its root. This character stillness — above, it can assist in the work of transformation and nurture; below, it can embrace all things. I proclaim this stillness for you: it is not only useful for cultivating the Way and waking, but even for ordering the family and governing the state it is indispensable!

In this one character stillness the subtlest principle is inexhaustible. Yet those who speak of stillness are many, while those who know it are few; hence they desire stillness but cannot attain it, because they have not found the root of stillness. The root of stillness is first to see the world as empty. The gate of stillness lies in the place of not-yet-still, where one does the work of cutting off utterly. The end of stillness is to be used in the constant stillness.

The wondrous method of guard and defense: as soon as a thought arises, immediately destroy it. When destroyed and it grows again, do not let it grow. When born, at once destroy it, so that it is destroyed forever. At the extreme of stillness, non-stillness is stillness of itself. When does it speak of stillness, and when does it speak of non-stillness?

To rest in the highest good, nothing surpasses stillness. In stillness: before Mount Tai crumbles one is not alarmed — not that one deliberately is unalarmed, but that before the crumbling is as before the crumbling had never come; before a beauty one does not stir — not that one deliberately does not stir, but that her presence is as if she were not present. As for movement and conduct, in receiving others and handling things, such is the merit of composure that it holds what one does not know why.

To parents, the willful become kind; to brothers, the fierce become harmonious; to wife and children, the violent become obedient; to friends, the false become sincere; to the vulgar, the coarse become refined; to scholars, the unruly become restrained. With this to serve one's lord, loyalty is of one's inborn nature; with this to love the people is true love, not a weak indulgence. What way is there that cannot be practiced, what resolve that cannot be extended?

This is not strange, yet its strangeness cannot be spoken. Not only is there stillness in stillness, but also stillness in movement; where movement and stillness are both still, the Way can be accomplished. The Buddhists speak of illuminating the mind and seeing the nature; without stillness one cannot illuminate or see. The Confucians speak of exhausting principle and actualizing the nature; without stillness one cannot exhaust or actualize. The Taoists speak of cultivating the true and nourishing the nature; without stillness one cannot cultivate or nourish. Stillness is the vital pulse of the three teachings. And this is not all. Look at a single day: without the stillness of night there is no ground for the movement of day. Through the four seasons: without the stillness of winter there is no ground for the movement of spring. Thus the Way is rooted in stillness — the natural pattern. The Way is itself natural; apart from stillness, from where does one enter?

Master Chongyang said this stillness is a practice inseparable from the three teachings. Scholars, farmers, artisans, merchants, princes, marquises, generals and ministers — all must attain stillness, and only then can they be at rest; being at rest, they can deliberate; deliberating, they can attain. If parents can be still, the child is filial of itself. If the sovereign can be still, the minister is loyal of itself. If brothers can be still, they are harmonious; if friends can be still, they are trustworthy; if husband and wife can be still, they are compliant. He set this stillness before the disciples, well knowing that among these tens there were only Qiu, Liu, Wang, Tan, Ma, and Hao who were willing to concentrate on waking to the Way. The rest were all diligent at the start and slack at the end — with a beginning but no ending — and could not be counted as genuine cultivators; later they would not escape the conduct of contending for fame and gain. So he spoke this work of composure to them, that they might gain the skill, temper away their waywardness, and practice self-cultivation. Though it be not the transcendence of the mortal to reach the sage, it can attune the body and order the family, and they need not fail to be good men, nor be disappointed at having come to take refuge.

Now Qiu Changchun, hearing the master expound this stillness so naturally and so thoroughly, with its many excellences, could not keep his heart from rejoicing, and he began to dance and caper. But this caught the master's eye, who pointed at Changchun angrily and said, "You fellow — you hear the Way and do not advance, you know the principle and do not awaken. You only show off your cleverness and make a display of your sharpness. You cannot bear to hide and cherish it; you only know to play the clever and be coy — you are no vessel for the Way! I have lectured several times and been overstepped by you. I shall now keep my distance from you in the southeast, lest you come continually to trouble me." Then he said to Ma Danyang, "Tomorrow I am going to Jiangnan to seek the Way. Only Liu Changsheng, Tan Changzhen, Hao Taigu, and Wang Yuyang will go with me; you may keep charge of the household affairs. As for the rest, let them go or stay as they please. On this journey, at most a year, at least half a year, before I return."

When the master issued these words, they stirred the disciples' longing for home. Some wished to return to see their parents, some to look after their children. Through the night they packed their bundles and luggage, and only waited for the sky to open its bright eyes; then they all came to take leave of Ma Danyang, entreating him to convey their respects to the master. Ma Danyang could but see them out of the estate, and they all bowed and parted.

Ma Danyang returned to the thatched hut. Master Chongyang bade him bring out five sleeve-robes, five rush cushions, Taoist caps, palm-leaf hats, straw sandals, hemp shoes, rock-gourds, and travel-spades — all such things. Master Chongyang, together with Liu, Hao, Wang, and Tan, all changed into Taoist attire, in the dress of the Taoist school; and taking advantage of the sky not yet fully bright, they quietly left Ma Family Estate.

Ma Danyang saw them out past the estate and returned; then he saw Qiu Changchun making a bow to take his leave. Ma Danyang asked where he was going. Qiu Changchun said, "I mean to follow the master." Ma Danyang said, "The master cannot bear the sight of you; that is why he has left. If you chase after him now, you will surely suffer." Qiu Changchun said, "The master does not truly find me unbearable; he only wishes me to become good. If I do not go, will I not betray his good heart?" So saying, he went. Ma Danyang called after him, "Come back quickly — I have something to say to you." But as to what was said, listen to the next section for the answer.
The others, longing home, each went their way; / Changchun, loving the master, hurried to stay.

blocks.text: 14. Testing the Ordinary Mind, Reprimands Repeatedly Given; Following the Master's Will, He Holds Constant Refuge

inline.s: To rid one’s evil is to loose a tangled skein; / The spirit-mind will find its hour and be free again;
But if one misapplies a little of one’s might, / For myriad aeons and a thousand births, no end in sight.

Now Ma Danyang called Qiu Changchun back and said, "The master and the elder Dharma-brothers have all changed into Taoist robes, and only then may they travel far. As you are, you are still dressed in a layman's clothes — how can you go? I have a patched robe and a Taoist cap; put them on and you can go!" Qiu Changchun was overjoyed at the words, and at once put on the patched robe and the Taoist cap, and taking up Ma Danyang's rush cushion, travel-spade, and rock-gourd all together, he set out after the master. After walking a while, he saw far off Tan, Hao, and the others following the master as they strolled. Changchun saw that in the countryside some folk were at breakfast, and thought to himself, "We set out early and have not eaten. Better that I go beg some alms to offer the master." He had never begged alms before and did not know how to do it. He hardened his face and stood at the door of a house, holding his rock-gourd in his hand. A yellow dog barked, and someone came out to look. Turning back inside, they brought a full bowl of millet rice and poured it into his gourd. Changchun, overjoyed, begged at two more houses. When the gourd was full, he carried it with both hands and hurried up to the master.

Now Master Chongyang walked a good while and stopped to rest under a great tree. He asked Liu, Hao, and the others, "Have you brought any travel money?" Liu Changsheng answered, "Because the master set out so hastily, we chased after and had not the time to ask Brother Ma for traveling money." The master said, "Since you have brought no travel money, each of you may go beg a meal; I will wait here." At these words the four each took their rock-gourds and went begging. Master Chongyang sat alone under the tree, when he saw Qiu Changchun come carrying a gourd of rice to offer the master. Master Chongyang said angrily, "Who told you to come and trouble me? I cannot accept this offering of yours!" Changchun pleaded again and again, but the master paid him no heed. Presently Liu, Hao, and the others each brought back some alms and asked the master to eat; the master ate a little of what Liu Changsheng had begged and then would take no more. When they had all finished eating, they rose together. They traveled on more than ten li, and as the light was fading they saw a cold temple by the roadside, and went in. They swept it clean, laid down their rush cushions, and sat in meditation the night through.

The next day the six, master and disciples, went on again. Qiu Changchun, following behind, begged alms along the road. When he met a good man of a house who called him in to eat, Changchun said, "I have my master ahead; he is old and has not eaten. How dare I enjoy it myself?" The good man said, "That is no trouble; go and eat, and I will prepare some clean vegetarian fare for you and fill your gourd, that you may carry it to him in time." Seeing the sense in this, Changchun went up to the table and ate his fill. Then he came down and thanked the good man, and indeed found the gourd filled with vegetarian fare; carrying it with both hands he hurried ahead. Seeing the master not far off, he only called, "Master, go slowly! Your disciple has brought your meal." Master Chongyang pretended not to hear and went straight on. Changchun took great strides to catch up and offered the food. The master looked at it and said, "This is the food of a single house; I have no merit to receive it. Have you not heard — one gourd of the food of a thousand houses, a lone body traveling ten thousand li?" Hearing the master's words, Changchun fell silent. In the twinkling of an eye the master had gone on ahead.

He thought of returning the food to the good man, but going and coming would cost him the road. He thought of eating it himself, but his belly was already full. With no recourse, he shouldered the gourd and came on behind. His two arms were numb and his whole body streaming with sweat, when he at last saw the elder Dharma-brothers seated with the master on a rock ahead, partaking of alms. Fortunately what they had begged was very little, so he straightway set this gourd of rice before them. Each took a little, and only so did they finish it. That night they lodged again in an old temple. Changchun thought to himself, "My master is a man of Shaanxi; he does not care much for rice, but loves steamed buns and noodles. Tomorrow I will beg a few buns to offer him."

That night his resolve was fixed, and the next day he indeed begged several white-flour steamed buns to offer the master. Master Chongyang said angrily, "I told you from the first I would not eat what you bring. Why do you plague me so?" So saying, he snatched the gourd and flung it to the ground, nearly cracking it. The steamed buns rolled down the slope, and Qiu Changchun hastened to pick up the gourd and gathered the buns back into it. When he looked, the master had gone far, and he straightway hurried after.

Reader, do you ask why Master Chongyang treated Changchun so insultingly? Because he had begun to study the Way in his youth, and was not like Liu, Hao, Wang, and Tan, who had already transformed their natures. Unless he was deeply polished, how could he be made into a vessel? This is exactly what is meant by grinding his disposition. Who would have known that Changchun, with a deep root and firm foundation, suffered rebuke time and again without the least resentment?

Master Wang Chongyang and his disciples, the several of them, traveled more than two months. At that time the weather was cold, and in the countryside they had begged a few bundles of firewood and straw. That night it rained and snowed, bitterly cold, so they took some of the kindling and lit a fire to warm themselves. The instant Master Chongyang saw it he grew angry within, and flung all those bundles of firewood into the fire. All at once it blazed up in towering flame, its sparks flying wildly. Master Chongyang, taking his travel-spade, pressed the firewood down a few times; the flame died at once, thick smoke billowed, and it choked them until they had nowhere to turn. The temple was small, and the wind blew inward, so Qiu and Liu and the rest, unable to bear the smoke, had no choice but to go out the gate to escape it. Each rubbing his brows and eyes, they all said, "What a choking smoke! What a choking smoke!" When the master saw they had gone out, he shut the gate, moved his rush cushion before the door, and sat with his back to it as a bar. They stood outside for a while, and the smoke no longer choked them, but then the cold seized them. They turned to push the door — how could it budge? Not daring to call out, they sat all together under the eaves. Suddenly a gust of snowy wind came, and the cold set the several of them shivering. Liu Changsheng said, "The master has taught us the fire exercise; why should we not all do it, to ward off the severer cold?"

Changchun and his fellow practitioners set to their work, closing the breath, gathering the qi, and moving it about. Before long they not only were not cold, but began to feel warm. After a while the sky grew bright, and seeing the temple gate open, they all went in. There was the master sitting on his rush cushion, his anger unabated, and he said to them, "You fear heat and dread cold; you cling to life and dread death. You abandon the true and seek the false, greedy to warm yourselves at a false fire, unwilling to turn the true fire. You crave only ease, and will not apply deep practice. With such sloth, how can you cultivate the Way to completion? If I do not chastise you heavily, in the end it will be diligence at first and sloth at the last." Then he ordered Wang Yuyang to bring the ruler, and every one of them was to be struck twenty times, to warn them for the future. Liu, Hao, and the others, hearing this, turned the color of clay and dared not reply. Qiu Changchun knelt before the master and said, "The fault is this disciple's alone; it has nothing to do with the elder Dharma-brothers. I am willing to take the punishment, and beg the master to spare them." The master said, "Since you are willing to bear it for them — at twenty each, the sum is one hundred strokes." Liu, Hao, and the others all came and begged for mercy. The master sighed, "You beg each other off — how could I not release you? But never again do this, lest you ruin your own prospects." So saying, he flung the ruler to the ground, and said to Liu Changsheng, "In a moment's impulse I resolved obstinately to wander south. Now that the interest is spent, I would still return north. Set out at once; let there be no hesitation."

So saying, he turned to go out. Qiu, Liu, and the others hurriedly rolled up their cushions, took up their spades, took leave of the old man who kept the shrine's incense, and then followed the master, taking the same road back to Shandong. Before long they reached the county of Ninghai and came to Ma Family Estate. Qiu Changchun first went in to tell Ma Danyang, and Danyang hurried out to welcome the master inside, where he lodged once more in the thatched hut behind. For a time there was nothing of note; no need to tell of it in detail.

After more than a month the disciples, hearing the master had returned, one by one came again to study the Way, and it grew lively once more. The master thought of a clever plan to send them away. How did he do it? Listen to the next chapter for the answer.
Unless the false intent be sent away, / How will the true heart come and wake the Way?

blocks.text: 15. Signifying Ascension, the Master Retires; Escorting the Coffin, the Disciples Labor

inline.s: Where the wind-stirred banner flutters, nought is true; / The pure bright nature is the Dharma-body too;
He who perceives the flower and the smile’s clear sense, / Finds not thereafter where a speck of dust may rest.

Now Master Chongyang saw that the seekers of the Way had again gathered. Examining them, he found none who truly turned his heart to the Way; they only clung to an empty fame, using the Way as a pretext, and wishing people to know they were cultivating and waking, though in truth there was not a single thought of the Way in them. If he did not make them scatter, in time the false would confound the true, and the Dharma-gate could not be kept pure.

He thought of a clever plan, nodded his head, and suddenly called out loudly, "It is bad! It is bad!" Astounded, the people all crowded round to ask the reason. The master said, "I should not have gone out. On the road I took in the summer's heat and damp, so that my heart grew congested and blisters rose on my body." He opened his robe and showed them, and indeed his heart was swollen and his whole body covered in blisters. Alarmed, Ma Danyang and Qiu and Liu all hastened to find a physician and a cure. They invited one famous doctor after another, used several doses of wonderful medicine, but none did the least good. After two more days the blisters festered and broke, with pus and blood flowing and a stench hard to bear. Those who had come to study the Way and cultivate said secretly among themselves, "Master Chongyang surely has no Way. One who cannot protect himself, how can he save others? He cannot even be rid of an illness — how can he become an immortal? We had best go back, each of us, lest we waste our time on a lost cause." Thereupon, one slipping away quietly, another openly, in less than two days they were gone clean, leaving only Qiu, Liu, Tan, Ma, Hao, and Wang — the six — to attend him day and night.

When the master saw that the crowd had all gone, he called the six of them near and directed them, "At noon tomorrow I will surely die. But since I came here, the silver in Ma Yu's household I used to succor the poor and needy, and to help others with burials and weddings, and to give serving-girls away in marriage, and to finish the trousseaus and betrothal-gifts for the young men of the household — a good deal of silver was spent. And I supported those who came to study the Way for a year or two, and so the silver was all used up. Now the storehouse is empty. When I die, if a funeral is to be held, land must be pledged and sold. But follow my instruction and spend no money. When I die, you need not grieve and wail, and there is no need for offerings and mourning-visits. Only take a few thin boards to contain this stinking skin-bag, and let the five of you, Qiu, Liu, Wang, Tan, and Hao, carry it back in turn to Chū (
chū

) county of Shaanxi, beneath Mount Zhongnan. Where the rope breaks is the place of my burial — you must not err. If you go against my words, I shall not rest at peace." Hearing the master's words, Qiu and Liu and the others choked and wished to weep. Master Chongyang said, "Do not work yourselves up into this child's mood!" Though the master directed them so, Qiu, Liu, and the others could but harbor sorrow and give rise to grief — of this there is no need to speak.
At noon the next day the master, in well-ordered dress, sat upright upon his rush cushion, called the six, Qiu, Liu, Tan, Ma, Hao, and Wang, near, and expounded the Way:

The method of cultivating together nature and lifespan requires both the outer and the inner. If the outer merit is lacking, the virtuous nature is incomplete; if the inner merit is lacking, the source and root are not clear.

As for the outer merit: throughout one's life, in all one's inward bearing, one must see to it there is no shortfall. Each word must be guarded — words have their merit; each act must be careful — acts have their merit. Each matter must not be careless; even a single trifle (meaning the smallest quantity, e.g., a single act of kindness) must be held strict about. There is nothing that is not the accumulation of merit, the advancing of merit.

What then is the inner merit? Watchfulness should not sink into dullness; guard the intent as one guards a city's danger. In blankness, alight on not a single thing; guard the mind more strictly than one guards the body. At times the heavenly and the human stand a hair apart (differing by the merest fraction), and that hair's breadth is where they do battle.

Let me set the inner merit forth with emphasis. The inner merit cannot be seen in form, cannot be sought in appearance, cannot be had by luck, cannot be gotten by slack ease. Sweep away a hair's worth of form and there is a hair's worth of yang as master; sweep away countless forms and there is countless yang born. Sweep the forms utterly clean, leaving not the least (a speck of) taint, and it is the body of pure yang.

There are some cultivators of the Way who are not lacking a firm faith, but whose fault lies in wanting quick success: before the work is done, they think of attaining the fruit. There are others who practice my Way who do not fail to apply their care, but whose fault lies in indolent ease: day after day they drowse as if to sleep, hour after hour depressed and joyless; their spirit lacks vigor, they find it hard to carry on the practice, and will not apply themselves. Do they not know that even a single skill and a single craft requires exhausting the mind's boundless contrivance before it can be used at will; even a half-thread and a half-silk requires spending a great deal of effort before it satisfies the heart? How then can those who would learn to be immortals fail to undergo bitter toil?

When Master Chongyang had finished, he took a book, named the Collected Works of Concealment of Light. It was written by his own hand, and within it were the way of concealing one's traces and the wonder of withdrawing into seclusion. He gave it to Ma Danyang and said, "You six should search its pages for the ultimate principle. To know it is not hard; to practice it is hard. Make sure you strive to practice it, and do not betray my heart. Your fellow practitioner Sun has a fruit of the Way nearly ripe; give him no more thought. Only Qiu Changchun has too few merits and practices; you should guide him a little. Liu Changsheng has not yet emptied his forms of appearance, and another wave of troubles awaits him. Hao Taigu, going east and returning west, the place he sees is the place where he concludes the Way. Tan Changzhen, meeting a Gu, will penetrate the mystery. Wang Yuyang, meeting a Yao, will enter the subtle. Qiu Changchun, by the edge of the Panshi stream the bitter root is exhausted; at the Dragon-flying gate the great elixir is complete." When Master Chongyang had spoken, he smiled and passed away.

Qiu, Liu, and the others reverently obeyed the master's last instructions, not daring to proclaim it abroad, and encoffined him according to the rite. They bound the coffin with ropes, found a carrying-pole and two cross-bars. The next morning Qiu, Wang, Tan, and Hao — four of them — shouldered the coffin and set off. Liu Changsheng carried the luggage behind. Ma Danyang saw them on their way more than twenty li; when they parted, he took from his side a pouch of small broken silver, about forty or fifty taels, and gave it to Liu Changsheng, saying, "The silver of the household was spent by the master in good works, so I could not raise more at once. Take this little broken silver as traveling money; if you are frugal on the road it will be enough. After you have buried the master, come back quickly, and we, fellow practitioners of the same school, will cultivate together in one place." Liu Changsheng took the silver and parted from Danyang. They had not gone a few li when they saw a crowd holding inch-long incense and scraps of paper, blocking the road with offerings. Liu Changsheng drew near and saw that they were all those false cultivators who had studied the Way among the master's disciples. Liu Changsheng thanked each in turn, but who would have thought — whereas during his life Master Chongyang could never abide false cultivators of the Way, now in death his true spirit did not sleep, and at the sight of them was still offended; from within the coffin it sent forth a blast of stench, so foul that everyone covered his nose, each retched, and could no longer stand upright. They knocked a few random head-bows and all went off, and the stench subsided.

Qiu Changchun and Hao Taigu and the others, bearing the coffin, went on westward. Before they had walked ten li, someone blocked the road and offered them a meal. Qiu and Liu and the others took it for someone who had known the master in former years, and who now, hearing the master had gone to heaven, had specially brought a meal to show a human kindness — no wonder. They quickly set down the coffin and came to eat. When they were done they said a word of thanks, shouldered the coffin again, and went on. Before long they saw an old temple by the roadside; no longer able to carry it, they set the coffin down on the flat ground and lodged in the temple that night. At daybreak the next day, having borne it to the time of breakfast, again someone blocked the road and served a meal. At lunchtime it was the same. When it was late they found a cold temple to put up in. So they went for more than a month and reached the border of Shaanxi. Qiu Changchun thought to himself, "Is this not strange! In all heaven and earth, how could such a coincidence happen? Nearby, one might suppose it was someone known to the master, doing a kindness; that is not beyond reckoning. But now after so great a distance, still someone blocks the road to offer a meal — the matter is truly extraordinary." He was musing to himself when, at noon, someone brought a meal and asked them to eat. Liu, Hao, Wang, and Tan thanked the man and took up bowls and chopsticks to eat. Qiu Changchun pulled the bearer aside and asked, "How did you know we would come here? And what is your reason for bringing us this meal?" The bearer said, "This morning an old Taoist in a yellow robe came begging alms in our village and said, 'I have five disciples bringing a coffin from Shandong, and they will pass this way; they wish to trouble some household for a meal.' My master is the most charitable, and hearing this he sent me with this meal."

Changchun took this to heart. The next morning, at the time of breakfast, he pretended his belly ached and said he had to go to the village ahead to beg a bowl of hot soup. He asked Liu Changsheng to help carry a share. Changsheng agreed, handed him the luggage, took up the pole, and shouldered the coffin. Qiu Changchun, carrying the luggage on his back, strode ahead several li and indeed saw an old man in a yellow Taoist robe, bearing something like the master's countenance, going into the village ahead. Qiu Changchun hurried a few steps, caught up, seized the robe with one hand, knelt down, and cried, "Master, go slowly — your disciple is here waiting upon you." Master Chongyang turned around, his face full of anger, and scolded Changchun, "You sin-making disciple! You do not know the way of the fullness and emptiness of heaven and earth, of the waxing and waning and the concealing of traces. You only show your cleverness and let slip the immortals' secret. Judging from this, you will have to spend yet another three years at the work of subduing demons — you bring this on yourself." So saying, he turned into a clear wind and was gone.

Changchun was in the midst of his remorse when he saw the coffin come up; he hurried to take the pole and shoulder it, and gave the luggage back to Changsheng. From then on, no one ever again brought a meal. Had it not been for the silver Ma Danyang had given them as traveling money, they could hardly have escaped starving.

After half a month more they reached Zhongnan. Suddenly their ropes all broke at once and the coffin fell to the ground. Changchun looked, and saw an old man standing at the head of the village before them; he went up and made a bow. Before the words left his mouth, the old man asked, "Are you the ones who have carried a coffin back from Shandong?" Qiu Changchun answered, "Just so. How did you know, uncle?" The old man said, "Last night I dreamed of Wang the successful candidate, who said he was dead. Five disciples bore his coffin from Shandong to this place, and begged me to give a plot of ground to bury him. I thought how in old days I sat the provincial examination with him in the provincial capital, and the two of us were great friends, so I agreed readily. I asked him when he was to be buried, and he said at noon today. I woke and knew it was a dream, half-believing and half-doubting, and came out to look several times, and only now see you bearing the coffin, which has just come to rest on this old man's land." Changchun then told the old man the master's words, that where the rope breaks is the place of his burial. The old man was much pleased, and went in to call out a few farmhands, each with a digging-spade and basket, and they came to the coffin. They moved the coffin over, dug a shaft at that place, and buried it, and in a moment raised a great mound. Qiu, Liu, and the others bowed thanks to the old man and thanked the farmhands for their pains. The old man then invited the brothers into the village and entertained them to a vegetarian meal. Thereupon Qiu, Liu, and the rest took leave of the old man, and having asked the way to the village of Daxiao, made a bow and went. What came of this journey? Listen to the next chapter for the answer.
The Master escorted westward, the great work done; seeking the Way eastward, the true path won.

blocks.text: 16. The Three Elders of Dawei Village Talk of Old Times; One Word at the Jin'an Bridge Points Out the Lost Path

inline.s: Turn a thousand times and still the heart is a boat that stays unmoved; but when the wind rolls and the waves heave, the craft is hard to hold.
Face the rushing current, hold fast the rudder and the helm; with a light sail all the way, glide at last to the shore.

Qiu Changchun and his elder fellow disciples came to Dawei Village in Xianyang and found the houses in ruins and the hamlet desolate. Three old men were seated at the gateway of a shrine. Changchun stepped forward and made a deep bow, then asked the way to the dwelling of the Filial-and-Incorrupt Gentleman Wang. One of the elders, whose beard and hair were all white, said, “You ask for the residence of Wang the Filial and Incorrupt — can you have some connexion with him?” Qiu Changchun replied, “He was our master. He spread the Way in Shandong and, his feathered transformation accomplished, ascended as a transcendent. The several of us have escorted his spirit-coffin back and yesterday sought ground beneath the Southern Mountain to lay him to rest. Now we were to return to Shandong, so we have come to ask after his household. Are they safe and well?”

At these words the old man sighed and said, “Your master is my elder cousin of the same clan. I am third in seniority, and so people call me Wang San Lao. Ever since my cousin left home, his wife née Zhou fretted herself into illness and died of it. His son Qiulang went off with his father-in-law, returning once every half year or so, so that now there is no one in the household.” Changchun asked, “How has the village fallen into such ruin?” Wang San Lao sighed again and said, “After my cousin left, there was no one in the village to take charge of affairs; each man looked only to himself. When matters arose, there was no one to step forward and set them in order, so men simply let themselves be dragged along by others. Thus things grew worse and worse, the more cunning the poorer, and in the end the village was ruined. Afterwards, when folk heard the Filial and Incorrupt had become a transcendent, they all said he had carried off the vital spirit of the land and lightly laid the blame upon him.”

Changchun asked again, “How do you know he became a transcendent?” Wang San Lao pointed to the shrine and said, “This is the temple that the several villages south and north built for him; go in and look for yourselves.” Changchun and his elder fellow disciples entered the hall and saw the Master's image enshrined above, as lifelike as in life; and they all went up together and bowed. They saw the four characters “Zhenghu Renhao” written on a framed plaque, while the couplet flanking it read: “He displayed his art in Xianyang, holding wine in his mouth and spraying it out (
xùn
, that is, to take liquid into the mouth and spurt it forth) to quench the fire; he poured his gracious light upon his homeland and issued talismans to drive off the plague.”

Qiu, Liu and the rest had read it through, yet did not understand its meaning, so they asked the three elders how he had driven off the plague and quenched the fire. San Lao said, “That year plague was rampant in our region and spread heavily, so that every soul was terrified. Suddenly there appeared a Daoist priest in yellow garments, who wrote efficacious talismans in vermilion and distributed them throughout the villages, never taking a single coin. Whoever obtained one of these talismans and pasted it on the door found the plague at once dissipated. Again, folk said that a fire broke out in the market of Xianyang and caught the people's houses, and that none could put it out. They saw a Daoist, also in a yellow robe, come out of a tavern with a half-cup of wine held aloft in his hand. He took a sip and sprayed it toward the fire, and the fire went out of itself. The townsfolk, moved by his deed in saving them from the blaze, all came to ask his name. He answered, “Three horizontals end-to-end is my surname; three scholars with open mouths make my name.” Having spoken, he drifted away and in the twinkling of an eye was gone. Afterwards some wisehead unravelled the two phrases: three horizontals end-to-end spell “Wang”! Three scholars with mouths spell “Zhe”! They said he must be Wang Zhe. This talk reached our village, and only then did we know he had become a transcendent. We had a cousin of our own clan, known as Mama Wang, who at her dying breath also said, “Uncle, the Filial and Incorrupt, dressed in yellow, has come to take me away.” For this reason the villages south and north, mindful of the grace of his protection, have taken the lead in building this shrine to repay his virtue. On the left wall hangs a wooden board recording the deed; one look and you will understand.”
Liu, Qiu and the others went together below the board, and looking up, read its inscription, which said:

It has long been heard that those who labour for the state are honoured with sacrifice, and those who render merit to the people are honoured with sacrifice. Our worthy Grandfather Wang, whose given name was Zhe, was a man of the extraordinary. In youth he studied letters; in maturity he practised the martial arts. After he was recommended as a Filial and Incorrupt, he feigned illness so that he could not speak. No one could fathom his movements; for twelve years he nourished his ailment without once stepping out to gaze afar. One day he vanished, and none knew whither he had gone. Search was made in all directions, yet no trace of him was found. Afterwards plague arose, and the gentleman distributed talismans to save the folk, preserving not a few lives, so that the whole countryside shared in his grace. Again, in the market of Xianyang he spat wine to extinguish a fire and left his name behind in a riddle. He guided his widowed sister-in-law to ascend to heaven and bestowed much fortune on the villagers. Since the gentleman did not forget his own village, how could the villagers turn their backs upon him! Moreover, having the merits of driving away plague and quenching fire, it is fitting that the people should offer him sacrifice. Therefore we have gathered the villagers in common deliberation and taken the lead in building this hall and erecting his image, that at the seasons of the year we may offer sacrifice to repay his toil. Thus we say this.”

Qiu and Liu, having read it, sighed and said, “How unfathomable is the Master's divine foresight, how inexhaustible his transformations — far beyond what we can comprehend!” Then they saw Wang San Lao whisper something into the ear of a young servant; no one knew what words he spoke, but the boy nodded and went off. Before long he returned with a farmhand, carrying a woven basket — pronounced
lǒng
— filled with cakes and the like, and set it before the fellow seekers to enjoy.

Liu and Qiu had no sooner begun to speak a word of thanks when San Lao said, “I have put you to the trouble of escorting my cousin's spirit-coffin back to his homeland and of coming again to inquire after his family. I have nothing fine to offer, only a plain meal, which hardly deserves your thanks.” Seeing him speak thus, Qiu and Liu sat down to eat. That night they lodged in the shrine, and many came to call on them. At daybreak the next morning food was sent from seven or eight quarters. How could their few fellow seekers eat so much? They took only a little from each household, to acknowledge its kindness.

Liu Changsheng consulted with the fellow seekers: they took the more than ten taels of travelling silver that Ma Danyang had given them and handed it to San Lao, to be used for repairing the Master's shrine. All the fellow seekers approved of this. Thereupon they gave the silver to San Lao and explained their purpose. Wang San Lao received it, and Qiu, Liu and the others took their leave and set out.

Leaving Dawei Village, they went on more than ten li to a great tree and sat down to rest awhile. Tan Changzhen said, “Escorting the Master westward, we have finished the great matter. If we were to go on to Shandong, it would be only to eat a few of Elder Brother Ma's meals and spend a little of his money. As the saying goes, “No feast in the world does not break up.” It is also said, “The Way does not cling to feeling; to cling to feeling is not the Way.” If we travel so long together, shall we not be seen as “three making a company, five forming a faction,” which only stirs gossip and is greatly to our inconvenience? Better that each go his own way, and so gain his freedom.” Wang, Hao and the others said, “What Elder Brother says is right.” So Liu Changsheng went off to the southeast, Wang Yuyang toward the southwest, Tan Changzhen headed south, and She Taigu east. Qiu Changchun, seeing the several roads all taken, found nowhere to go, and there in the Shaanxi region he begged for his keep and practised with a firm resolve. Of this we will say nothing for now.

Now of She Taigu alone it is told that he wandered into the region of Jin and saw a stone bridge of some eight or nine arches. Beneath it the foundations were bedrock born of the earth, and whenever autumn and winter came and the river ran dry, the famished refugees who had fled calamity would shelter there. She Taigu saw that under the bridge it was very clean, and since it was just then the season of low water, he sat in meditation beneath it. At first no one knew he was there, and so it was quiet. But by and by people gradually came to know of it, and this drew entanglements upon him. The nearby residents, moved that he sat in meditation from morning to night, recognised him for a man of practice, and so often brought him steamed buns and flat cakes. How could he eat so much? What remained he piled before him. The sparrows and crows seized upon it, each pecking a scrap and flying up, only to let the morsel fall into the water or drop onto the road. When the little children saw it, they picked it up and ate. Following the track and catching at the shadow, they came under the bridge and played before Taigu. Seeing him sit motionless, like a figure moulded of clay or carved from wood, the children, once grown familiar, took him for a bodhisattva and set about building him a shrine. They gathered stones and broken tiles and stacked them on both sides for walls, broke off branches to serve as beams, and pulled grass to cover it with. Each day after eating at home they would call one another and troop down under the bridge, where they kowtowed and made obeisance to She Taigu, laughing and shouting and raising an endless racket. She Taigu was a man of deep forbearance; he paid it no mind, and let them tumble about, squabble, and leap as they would, never once attending to them. This too may be counted as finding stillness amid clamour, and was not without benefit.

One day the nearby village held a Guanyin Lotus-Seat festival. The little children had all gone to watch it, and the place was very quiet. She Taigu saw a man under the bridge polishing a brick: he would rub it a while, then hold it up to his face to look; look, then rub; rub, then look again; and so on some dozens of times, until he had worn one brick away, whereupon he took up a second to polish. Taigu, seeing him toil half the day, thought he meant to grind the brick into some vessel. Now that he saw the man reduce the brick to mud to no purpose whatever, and then begin polishing a second, he feared the man was wasting his labour and was minded to point the way for him. So he asked the brick-polisher, “In polishing this brick, do you mean to make some vessel of it?” The man answered, “Just so.” She Taigu then said to him, “If you would make a vessel, you must first hold a set purpose in mind: either pare away the high and smooth the low, or take what is square and bring it to round. Only by following the compass and the square can you achieve a fine result. Now you follow no measure but grind at random — how can you succeed! Let me ask you, in the end what vessel are you making?” The man answered, “I thought to polish the brick bright and make a mirror of it, that morning and evening I might look upon my face.” At this She Taigu laughed and said, “A brick is but kiln-fired clay, neither bronze nor iron; how can it be polished bright? Are you not throwing away your labour?” The man laughed heartily and said, “By your own reasoning, even as my brick cannot be ground into a mirror, so your sitting — how can it bring you to transcendence? Your dry, fruitless sitting is no different from my polishing of a brick.” At these words She Taigu gave a violent start! He hastily rose and hurried forward, wishing to ask instruction; but the man drifted away and he could not speak with him. She Taigu knew that an extraordinary being had come to point out that dry sitting was no different. He packed his gear, left the Jin'an Bridge, and set out for the region of You and Yan (the northern part of present-day Hebei and the region of Liaoning). There is a poem lamenting it:
To grind a brick, how vain the toil must be; to sit in lone seclusion, breath runs dry.
Both alike are labours fruitlessly; one word of counsel clears the mazed eye.

Leaving aside She Taigu's journey north, we go on to tell of Changzhen's journey south. One day he reached the region of Suizhou (in the north of present-day Hubei). The day was drawing to a close, and there was neither old temple nor cool pavilion, nor any inn to take in a traveller. He saw by the roadside a great manor with many rooms, and meant to go and ask lodging for the night, and in the course of it to beg a little vegetarian fare. Just as he was approaching the gate, a man came out from within, looking like the manager of the estate. This man was surnamed Gu, named Zucheng, with the style name Yufeng. In former years he too had been fond of the Way, but because idle fellow seekers had played at being immortals to swindle his money, and he had been taken in several times, he could not abide the sight of a Daoist. It is just as the saying runs: he who is struck by a fistful of sand from behind goes in fear of the man who follows.

Now Gu Yufeng, seeing Tan Changzhen approaching the manor, called out at the top of his voice, “Master, do not come here to my place! Monks and priests have no affinity with me!” Tan Changzhen cast a look at him, meaning to awaken him; but whether he would receive the teaching — listen to the next chapter for the answer.
If you would have others believe and trust in you, you must first make your own deeds worthy of trust.

blocks.text: 17. Teasing Xihong, He Devises a Plan to Slip Away; Confounding Hunranzi, the Way Is Truly Discussed

inline.s: The mind's own ground must by nature be bright and clear; let not one matter blight a whole life.
Deceived by counterfeit in former years; now that a genuine man appears, he is not recognised.

It is told that Tan Changzhen saw in Gu Yufeng something of a kindly spirit and was minded to awaken him. But Gu Yufeng, not waiting for him to speak, said first, “Master, you need say no more. I have grown weary of hearing such talk as yours. Even if you spoke, I should not believe you. I have been humbugged by your sort until I am afraid of you. Where is there truly a man of practice? As I see it, they are all fellows who merely scheme for food and clothing.” Having spoken, he went within and did not come out again.

Tan Changzhen, hearing these words that made the school of the Way seem wholly without the spirit of the Way, was minded to revive the tradition with all his might. He looked up and saw that night had fallen, so he sat in meditation at the manor gate. When it was fully dark, the farmhands came and pressed him to move on; they carried a bucket of cold water and drenched the gateway, then went back in and shut the door.

Seeing them behave so wickedly, Tan Changzhen did not go to their gate but sat in meditation by the roadside. That night it snowed again, piling up more than a foot deep. At dawn the farmhands came out and saw Changzhen seated in the open courtyard with white snow heaped all about him; yet, strange to tell, not so much as a single flake lay upon his person. They reported this to Yufeng, who came out himself to look. Stepping to his side, he felt a warmth of vital breath greeting him, and knew him for a man of the Way. He thereupon invited him within and treated him with the courtesy due a guest, saying, “It is not that I do not believe in the Way, but that the school of the Way has no good men in it. A venerable elder who practises with such bitter resolve — who would not revere him? I now wish to support you. Stay here in my house three years or five, ten years or eight — it would all please me. Tomorrow I shall choose an auspicious hour and take you for my master; I wonder whether you, venerable elder, will consent?” Tan Changzhen had meant to awaken him, and now saw that he had begun to stir a little faith in the Way, and it was not weak; how could he refuse? So he nodded his assent. Gu Yufeng, overjoyed, ordered a servant to sweep out a room at the rear and invite Tan Changzhen within to sit in contemplation upon the mystery. Each day vegetarian tea and vegetarian meals were provided without stint; and he had the maid Xihong constantly carry broth and water to Tan Changzhen — truly the Way is true and virtue precious, and its subtle principle without end.

Time passed swiftly, and more than half a year went by. He did not see Gu Yufeng come to seek the Way or ask of its principle, and he judged from his intentions that the man loved the Way as a thing to admire rather than to study. He only wished to keep another man supported by his bounty, to have him create merit and do the cultivating on his behalf, while he enjoyed the blessing of good fortune ready-made. Tan Changzhen saw through this device and no longer wished to be supported in the man's house; he repeatedly took his leave and meant to go. But Gu Yufeng pressed him to stay with all his heart, and how would he let him go? He gave orders instead to the members of the household to keep close watch over him. And so, though Changzhen tried to leave several times, they held him back. Since he could not get away, Tan Changzhen thought of a fine stratagem, and concluded that only in this way could he depart. By and by Xihong brought in his tea. Tan Changzhen deliberately pinched her wrist and said, “How white and clean your hand is — enough to make one adore it!” Xihong's cheeks flushed crimson, and she forced herself to answer, “It is white as lacquer; Master, do not tease me.” So saying she went out, straight to the upper chamber, and told the mistress of the Gu household. The wife at once said to her husband, “Master Tan has toyed with our maid; he is no true man of practice and should be sent away.” But Gu Yufeng would not believe it and said, “It is only that Xihong is tired of serving him and so has invented these idle tales.” Seeing her husband speak so, the wife scolded Xihong instead for a while, and Xihong dared say no more.

Two days later, Gu Yufeng, seeing Xihong carry tea to Tan Changzhen, followed behind her to spy for himself. He saw Changzhen clasp Xihong's hand with a winning smile and say, “This hand of yours is white as jade and soft as cotton — it is enough to make one love one to death!” Hearing this from without, Yufeng was greatly angered and meant to turn him out. But then he reflected that the man had often wished to leave and that he himself had repeatedly pressed him to stay; now to expel him would show him unkind. Better to write a few words and paste them on the wall, and let the man see them — if he had any tact, he would surely leave of his own accord. He would only tell the servants not to bar his way; that was a good plan. Leaving Gu Yufeng to his secret preparations, we tell how the next morning Tan Changzhen, having sat until after breakfast and seen neither tea nor water brought by Xihong, knew that his stratagem had taken effect. He went out to look and saw a paper slip pasted on the gate, with four lines written upon it:
All night the west wind drove the flying snow; he sat on the cold mat, his shadow leaning low.
Do not envy the jade-like hand tonight; recall the frog you once were, small and low.

Tan Changzhen read it, smiled to himself, and went into his room. Seeing ink and brush on the table, he took up the brush and came out again, and added four lines of his own to the paper slip. Having written, he went in and gathered his bundle, then ran straight out through the front hall, calling out his thanks twice; no one answered, and he went straight out the manor gate and headed south. He wandered for two years before returning north — but that is to come later, and here we leave it.

Now as for the servants of the Gu household, since their master had given word that when Tan Changzhen came out they need not bar him but let him go of himself, they all drew aside when they saw him come out, and only reported it to their master after he was gone. When he heard of it, Gu Yufeng came to the rear and found four more lines added at the end of the original slip. Which four lines, do you ask?
Say naught of snow and moon and wind-blown flower; an upright heart knows no slanting shadow's power.
Were it not for that jade hand so praised and cried, I'd bide a frog within the well, confined.

Now Gu Yufeng, on seeing these four lines, knew at last that Tan Changzhen's toying with Xihong had been but a stratagem to get away, and he sighed without cease. This tale we set aside to tell of Wang Yuyang, who, after parting from the fellow seekers at Dawei Village, wandered to the region of Fangzhou (present-day Fang County in Hubei). On the northern road of this Fangzhou lived an official surnamed Yao, named Chonggao, who had once been a deputy commander of the New Peace garrison. Having seen through the vanities of the world, he resigned his post and returned home, delighting in the pleasures of field and garden. All his life he was fondest of the Way, and whenever he met a renunciate it was like meeting a kinsman: whether the man had practice or not, he would talk with him awhile. Nearby stood a temple called the Temple of Meeting Immortals. Its abbot too was a Daoist, and monks and priests passing to and fro would often lodge there. He had given the abbot word in advance that whenever a man of genuine practice and virtue came by, word must be brought to him; and the abbot had promised to do so.

One day there came a practitioner who was neither monk nor Daoist, calling himself a man of the Way. He was forever showing off his miraculous powers before people, saying he was ninety-six years old, that he had met Zhang Sanfeng several times and Lu Dongbin on a number of occasions; that Bodhidharma was his master and Jidian his close friend, and that he too could sit in meditation a day or two without once lying down (that is, without sleeping, sitting day and night). That day he arrived at the Temple of Meeting Immortals and spoke of liberating boundless beings. The abbot found his words pleasing and asked his name, and he said his style was Hunranzi. The abbot at once led him to see the honourable Yao. The moment he was presented, he said: “Monks are hungry ghosts in the midst of form, and Daoists are demons of the vital breath; neither can achieve transcendence nor attain Buddhahood. Only if one is like me, able to see through all things and keep the dust of the world from touching him, can he be called a true practitioner. He who learns the Way from me will live several hundred years.”

At these words Yao Chonggao was greatly delighted, and took him for a master, keeping him in his house and providing for him. This old man spoke without the least restraint, belittling monks and Daoists in every sentence. The Daoist of the Temple of Meeting Immortals was present at the time, and hearing him rail against monks and priests felt aggrieved. He thought to himself, “How tactless this old man is! I recommended him in good faith that he might receive support, and he has no regard at all for my dignity, slandering monks and priests to my very face. Does he not know that he who lifts the tiles from the roof should look to the man beneath the eaves? He cares only that the honourable Yao should revere him, and thinks nothing of holding us in contempt. I must find a man who can truly sit in meditation, that this old fellow may be put to shame, and so my heart be satisfied.” Having resolved thus, he took leave of Yao and went back to his temple.

A few days later, as it happened, Wang Yuyang came to lodge there. The abbot, seeing his free and easy bearing, was sure he must be a man of the Way; and seeing that he sat in meditation all day with a clear and vigorous spirit, judged that if any man might refute the old fellow, it would have to be this one. He wished to explain the matter to him but feared he would not go. So he hit upon a plan and said to Yuyang, “A great practitioner has come to the household of the honourable Yao, one who can sit more than ten days without once lying down. I should like to go with my fellow seeker and pay him a visit; what do you think of it?” Wang Yuyang was delighted to hear it, and went with the abbot to the Yao mansion. The gatekeeper went in and announced them, and Yao Chonggao came out himself to welcome them and brought them to the reception hall to take tea.
Before they could begin to talk, a white-haired old man came in. Wang Yuyang looked at him: the fellow had coarse brows and narrow eyes, an upturned nose, and high cheekbones (
quán

), with his lips and teeth thrust forward. Square of face and long of ear, he trailed a few wispy beard-hairs and showed a scant scattering of white hair on his head, so that he looked like an old crone. He came in and sat down in the seat of honour. The abbot said to Wang Yuyang, “This venerable gentleman is the great practitioner of whom I spoke.” At this Wang Yuyang stepped forward to make his salutation. The old man sat there quite unmoved, holding Yuyang in no esteem whatever, and said, “Tell me, fellow seeker — did you plant a flower, or did you plant a willow?” Wang Yuyang was wholly at a loss and did not answer. The old man asked again, “Have you a wife?” Wang Yuyang thought his questions merely vulgar and so answered offhand, “I do have a wife, but she is left at home, parted from me now.” Hunranzi gave a great guffaw and said, “You have left home for nothing! You do not know even so much. Let me teach you: “to plant a flower” is to leave home while young; “to plant a willow” is to leave home in middle age. When I asked whether you had a wife, I meant, have you come by the tidings of the true yin? You answered me in worldly speech, which shows you do not understand. And if I asked you of “conceiving a child,” you would know even less!”

Though Hunranzi insulted a man to his face, Wang Yuyang did not take it to heart; but how could the abbot's face keep its colour? Seeing the abbot flush crimson with shame, Yuyang could not but argue a little, that the dignity of all present might be saved. So he smiled and asked, “Just now the venerable gentleman spoke of the “true yin” — what thing precisely is the true yin? He spoke too of “conceiving a child”; but I know not in what place the child is conceived, nor what it is that is carried.” Hunranzi could not for the moment answer, and forced a smile, saying, “The mysterious mechanism may not be divulged; how could I lightly speak of it with the likes of you?” The abbot, seeing the old man force these words and knowing he was ignorant, said to Wang Yuyang, “Pray go on and speak, fellow seeker; I judge he knows nothing. There is no need to ask him.” But what was it that Wang Yuyang said? Hear the next chapter for the answer.
Oft he boasted in mighty terms; at a single question, no reply.

blocks.text: 18. Wang Yuyang, With the True, Subdues the False; Tan Changzhen, Telling of the Past, Warrants the Present

inline.s: They tell that in the Western Land a lotus rare is sown; blooms ten fathoms high, the root-stock like a boat is grown.
The mind's own altar bears the Jetavana tree; this very ground is Buddha's heaven to see.

It is told that with a few essential words Wang Yuyang refuted Hunranzi, so that he could not answer. The abbot, standing by, clapped his hands and laughed aloud, urging Yuyang to go on and speak and not be hard on the man, for he judged that he could not know it. Hunranzi, seeing the abbot say he knew nothing, began to take offence; but Wang Yuyang at once explained, “It is not that the venerable gentleman does not know — it is that he is unwilling to speak! Let me presume to set forth the principle, that we all may weigh it and see whether it be so. The “true yin” and the “true yang” are the two breaths of yin and yang. The true yang breath is stored in the liver, and the true yin breath is gathered in the lungs. The liver is wood, the dwelling of the soul; the lungs are metal, the abode of the earthly spirit. Metal is the Dui maiden and wood the Zhen youth; wood flourishes in the east and metal is born in the west. Therefore one likens them to the young man of the eastern house and the maiden of the western house. Now would one make metal and wood meet — the soul never leaving the earthly spirit, the earthly spirit never leaving the soul, as a husband cleaves to his wife and a wife to her husband — this is the principle of the union of yin and yang, and it is exactly what the venerable Hunranzi meant when he asked me whether I had a household. Yet one must borrow the Yellow Matron to lure them into meeting before they can see each other. The Yellow Matron is the true intention: by intention one accords with intention, and then metal and wood are both without separation, and so they attain the harmony of husband and wife. Intention belongs to earth and is full of feeling; its colour is yellow and it is fond of motion, whence it is likened to an old woman. Coming and going between east and west, it brings the two houses into communication, just like a matchmaker.
