As for “conceiving a child,” it is to say that the true breath congeals within the lower elixir field, as though with child. When the true breath is complete it manifests in spirit, and so it is said that spirit is the child of breath and breath the mother of spirit; hence comes the talk of the descent of the infant. When one reaches this point, the great elixir is accomplished, and one may grow old together with Heaven and Earth and share the rest of sun and moon.”

When the honourable Yao heard these words, his praise knew no end. Hunranzi, fearing that Wang Yuyang would snatch the rice-bowl from him, said grandly, “He who has virtue must have words, but he who has words need not have virtue. If you dare to sit in meditation with me and go two or three days without touching tea or water, then you may be said to have attainment.” Wang Yuyang smiled and said, “For longer than that, this humble one cannot sit; but two or three days — I am glad to keep you company.” Thereupon the two began to vie in the practice.

They spread felt and padded mats in the reception hall and sat side by side. Hunranzi had naturally been able to sit two or three days without tea or water; but because he was to be tested against Yuyang, a spark of resentment had lodged in his heart, and this made him unable to sit in peace and bred troubles without end. At one moment he thought of asking for tea, at the next he must go out and relieve himself, so that in a single day he left his seat several times. By the second day he could sit no longer, and actually got down from the mat to seek food and drink, and fell into a doze, snoring thunderously. Wang Yuyang sat on resolutely until the third day before he left his seat, and then felt all the clearer and brisker of spirit for it.

The honourable Yao praised him repeatedly, saying, “Master, in the art of sitting the venerable gentleman is no match for you.” Wang Yuyang said, “It is not that the venerable gentleman is inferior to me; it is that his years are advanced, and in old age the breath weakens. Were I at his age, I fear I could not endure half a day.” When Hunranzi heard this, he was won over in his heart, and came again to talk with him; he no longer dared hold himself high and mighty, but by degrees grew humble and lowly.

Wang Yuyang stayed several days in the Yao household, and taught him a few sections of the dark work of cultivation, and the two were greatly taken with each other. One day Yuyang excused himself on the pretence of going to the Temple of Meeting Immortals to fetch his baggage, but once gone he did not return for several days. Yao Chonggao sent a servant to ask, and the abbot said he had left that very day. When the honourable Yao heard this he stamped his foot and sighed deeply, saying their affinity was thin. Even Hunranzi was somewhat loath to see him go.

Setting aside the matter of Wang Yuyang, we tell of Liu Changsheng, who after parting from his fellow seekers made a journey south and then went again to eastern Lu, where he cultivated with whole-hearted devotion on Mount Tai for three years, and so attained the true fruit. He ascended to the upper realm, was feasted in the Jasper Pool, and went to pay homage to the Queen Mother. He saw behind her a host of dozens of celestial maidens thronging together, of a beauty rare in the world, past all depiction and description, both lovely and to be longed for. Unable to check the stirring of a single thought, he stole a glance at the assembled maidens. The Queen Mother asked, “You gaze upon them — what is your intention?” Hearing the Queen Mother's words, Liu Changsheng knew he had transgressed propriety, and in trepidation begged pardon, prostrating himself and saying, “Your subject chanced to see the rainbow garments swirling and the bright sleeves outstretched, and in a moment of inadvertence cast a glance at the celestial maidens. In truth I had no other intent; I beseech your gracious countenance to forgive me.”

The Queen Mother reproved him, saying, “The distinction of self and other is still within you, and the marks of form are yet not emptied. Even if you have perfected the golden elixir, you cannot rise beyond the ordinary and enter the sacred. Descend once more to the mortal world and cultivate with bitter toil.” Thereupon she ordered a celestial official to escort him down. The official of the Southern Heaven, obeying the Queen Mother's command, led Liu Changsheng to the Southern Heaven Gate. Just as Changsheng was about to ride the clouds downward, the official had already given him a shove in the back, and he tumbled from the Southern Heaven Gate. Of a sudden he woke and knew it had all been a dream and an illusion. When he recalled the affair of the Jasper Pool, it was truly the fault of a single thought. And the Master Chongyang had once said of him: “In the elixir arts you excel in all things; only in the marks of form are you not yet empty.” Now that in his dream he had entered the Jasper Pool and heard the Queen Mother's reproof, it tallied exactly with the Master's words. But how was this task of cultivation to be done? He must descend the mountain and seek out a man of eminence to instruct him.

So he came down the mountain, and after travelling but a few days he met Tan Changzhen, and the two told each other of all that had befallen them. Liu Changsheng said, “Your refusal to be supported by the Gu household was no unrighteous thought; but my mistakingly gazing upon the celestial maiden at the Jasper Pool was no small error. Now I wish to cultivate emptiness of the marks of form, but I do not know where to begin.” Tan Changzhen said, “In the days of old, when Xu Jingyang was young, he was devoted to the chase. One day, hunting among the mountains, he let an arrow fly at a fawn. With the arrow in its body the fawn fled, and Jingyang led his family over the whole mountain in search of it, until he found two deer in a hollow. The fawn lay on the ground and the doe lay licking its wound. When the doe saw men come, she did not flee either, and both were captured. When they were taken home and unbound, both deer were already dead; and when their bellies were opened, the doe's bowels were found broken into inch-long pieces, while the fawn, though wounded, had its bowels quite whole. From this one may see that a mother's grief for her young is sharper far than the pain of the arrow itself. Seeing this, Jingyang's heart was stirred to pity; he broke up his bow and arrows, went into the mountains to cultivate, and so attained the true fruit. Wishing to convert and deliver all beings in the ten directions, he ascended a platform to proclaim the Dharma and gathered several hundred disciples.”

One day Jingyang said to his disciples, “You several hundred are not few in number, and your abandonment of home to study the Way is not lacking in devotion. But a man of practice must see through the marks of form. Can you look upon beauty without greed?” The disciples answered with one voice, “As for wealth, and anger, and wine, we may not have cast them all away; but as for the matter of lust, we have always taken it lightly and are not greedy for it.” Xu Jingyang said, “You speak so cleanly — I only fear it may not be so.” The disciples answered, “How would we dare speak falsely to deceive our master?” Xu Jingyang said, “I have a method that will test the truth of it. Let each of you prepare a piece of charcoal, more than two feet long, or three or four feet if you can, and set it on your bed to sleep with you for a night. When you rise tomorrow morning, bring it to me. Then if you have genuine attainment, I will transmit it to you.” The disciples, hearing this and not knowing the reason, each went to prepare a piece of charcoal and placed it on his bed.

That night, a disciple woke from his slumbers to find another sleeping beside him. When he reached out a hand and touched it, it was warm and soft as cotton, smooth as jade. Feeling further down the body, he found it was a woman. His desire blazed up suddenly and could not be curbed, and he gave himself over to it. Once his true yang had been shed, he still clung to her fondly and slept in her embrace. At dawn voices called from outside, “Bring the charcoal, come quickly — the master has been waiting a long while!” The disciples started from their dreams, and every one of them was holding a piece of charcoal in his arms. Just as they were wondering at this, the voices called again, and they could only dress and come to hand over their charcoal. Jingyang bade the disciples stand in two rows and come up one after another to present it. The disciples dared not disobey, so they stood in two rows, and one came forward to present his charcoal. Xu Jingyang asked, “How old are you?” The man said, “Your disciple is this year seventy-six.” Jingyang said, “At so great an age, why can you not see through the matter of lust?” The man answered, “How does your disciple appear not to see through it?” Jingyang said, “Since you can see through the matter of lust, then what is that which is smeared on your charcoal?” The man looked at his charcoal, and midway along it saw some faint white spots, the marks of a defilement. Only then did he realise it was the true yang he had shed the night before; feeling ashamed, he hung his head and dared not make a sound. Only then did the others understand that the woman with whom they had lain that night had been a transformation of the charcoal. When they looked at their own charcoal again, there were even more marks upon it. Afraid of being shamed before the rest, each stood frozen and would not bring up his charcoal; though urged again and again, none would stir. Only one man stepped forward smiling, and presented his charcoal with no trace upon it at all. Xu Jingyang asked, “Lust is what men delight in — why is it you do not care for it?” The man answered, “Your disciple has cultivated it out of the midst of lust itself.” Jingyang asked how he had done so, and he said, “Whatever one delights in, one must also fear. At first one fears he cannot get it; but once it is in hand, then from morning to night he takes his pleasure and will not stop. When a man is worn in spirit and weak in breath, and moreover frets over life and death, this is what makes him fear. When fear grows great he must flee from it, and so, meeting the object of his desire, he forgets his longing, and cuts off desire to preserve his life. In my youth I was dissolute and unrestrained, lying among the flowers and sleeping among the willows all day, and for a whole year I never went home. I made the house of pleasure my own home, and saw many beautiful dames and ladies, and tasted endless moons of pleasure and flowers of wanton bliss, until my spirit was wounded. I grew afraid and wished to flee, but could not escape; and so I fled here and studied the Way, wishing to preserve my life and no longer cling to beauty. There is no other trick in it than this, that having seen and known much, and having gone through it, one lets it go.” Xu Jingyang nodded at these words, and sent all the other disciples away, keeping only this one, to whom he transmitted the mystery of the Way; and in the end he too attained the true fruit. Judging from this, in all matters one must have seen and known much before the heart can hold them lightly and let them go.

When Tan Changzhen had finished this tale of the ancients, Liu Changsheng said, “I never had a mind for the inner practice; it was only that I delighted in their outward beauty. Some day I shall go to the house of pleasure and survey all the painted brows and powdered faces, until I have gained breadth of knowledge and experience, and my eyes are open and wide.” Tan Changzhen invited him to go to the region of Jin and see the birthplace of the Ancestor of the Way.

The two travelled on for many days, and on the way met Wang Yuyang, and the three went on together. Yuyang then told the two of the discourse on the Way he had had with Hunranzi at the Yao household. Liu Changsheng laughed and said, “It was cheap gain for that old fellow — the mystery of our Way was won by him.” Wang Yuyang said, “If I had not been able to sit in meditation, the old man would never have been convinced.” Tan Changzhen said, “So it seems. The practice of sitting is the staff that knocks at the gate for all who study the Way; whoever is of our school must learn it.” As the three walked and talked, they suddenly heard someone behind crying out, “How fast you have gone!” Who was this person? We must look to the next chapter to know.
That winsome form is but a rosy skull; Morning joy and evening mirth are never full;
Once impermanence at last arrives, all’s done; On the Night Terrace, old gallantry cannot run.
[Night Terrace: a grave; by extension, the underworld.]

blocks.text: 19. Discoursing on the Mysteries, Four Words Accord with Wondrous Truth; Hewing a Stone Cave, One Man Labors Alone

inline.s: Cultivation itself can reach the lofty shore; Why seek a boat midstream, and labor more?

As the story tells, Liu Changsheng, Wang Yuyang, and Tan Changzhen were walking together when they suddenly heard someone calling from behind. The three turned to look, and there was Hao Taigu. They greeted one another and exchanged news of their parting. Traveling on together, the four came to the district of Ku County (present-day Luyi County, Henan Province, the birthplace of Laozi) and found the place where Taishang (the Supreme Lord, the Taoist title of honor for Laozi) was born. There they saw nine wells encircling an octagonal pavilion, and beside the pavilion a plum tree, beneath which, as tradition says, Taishang was born. The four stepped into the pavilion, and in its center stood a stone stele recording the story of his birth. It read:

In the reign of Pangeng, the Shang was renamed Yin. In the fifth year of Yin, a family dwelt here, skilled in the principles of number, able to know past and future, and devoted to the work of pure quietude. All their lives they hid themselves away and sought neither fame nor office. This family had a daughter, nineteen years old, who had not chosen a husband. Meek and retiring by nature, she took no pleasure in laughter or talk. One day she chanced beneath the plum tree and, seeing a single plum upon the branch, fresh and red and lovely, she plucked it and swallowed it, and so conceived a child. Because a maiden had conceived without a husband, there arose some idle talk. The family, examining the principles of number, knew that a great sage was to be born into the world, and so they tended her with care, and she came to no harm.”

“The holy embryo grew within her, and she chose the year and month for its birth. When she found a good year there was no good month, and when she found a good month there was no good day, and when she found a good day there was no good hour. Choosing and choosing again, she chose for eighty-one years. By then the holy mother had passed a hundred years, carrying the holy embryo, neither hungry nor cold, free of sickness and harm. On the fifteenth day of the second month of that year she went beneath the plum tree to while away her sorrow, and Taishang rent his mother’s left side and came forth. He was born with white hair, and as soon as he touched the ground he could walk. He took seven steps forward and three steps back, and cried aloud three times: ‘Above the heavens and below, I alone am the honored one.’ When he had made this cry, there came from mid-air the sound of immortal music, clear and loud, a fragrant wind drifting by, and jade maidens scattering flowers. Nine dragons spouted water to bathe his body, and where the water fell, nine wells were formed. Taishang’s wisdom was without equal and his holy virtue like unto Heaven; he took the plum tree as his surname. Because he was born with white hair, the people of the time called him Laozi (the Old One) — such is the account of his birth. His other wonders are recorded in the classics and the histories, verified by generation after generation, not without basis.”

When Liu and Hao and the others had finished reading, they praised him: “The Way of Taishang, his legacy and his model, endures through a thousand autumns and is extolled through ten thousand ages; our hearts cannot dwell on him enough. You and I have awakened to the Way for many years, yet who can say whether our mystic work is worse or better? Facing this immortal scenery, let us freely reveal the mysteries of our attainment.”
Hao Taigu said:
The sword of wisdom hangs on high, the stars grow cold, The throng of demons, hands all bound, no tale unfold;
The cushion sits through the third watch’s moon, The elixir ninefold-turned, where dragon and tiger croon.
Wang Yuyang said:
In the immortal pavilion, reviewing the past, we speak of cold and warm, Verifying the mystic craft, we reach the truest norm;
Once the Golden Crow and Jade Hare are caught with all our might, The tiger crouches and the dragon coils, in nature’s right.
Tan Changzhen said:
The Dharma is boundless, making god and ghost feel chill, To rise past mortal and enter sagehood—can it lack a cause and will?
One fist shatters the net of delusion’s spell, Within the crescent furnace the dragon and tiger dwell.
Liu Changsheng said:
To raise the subject chills one’s very heart and gall, Where the rainbow robes are fluttering, the trouble first befalls;
The clever only end as deluded men, What need to speak of fairy mountains and the dragon’s den?

When the four had finished, Wang Yuyang asked again: “The words of us three all accord with the subtlety of the Way! We speak of victory and not defeat; yet why does Brother Liu speak not of victory but of defeat, dampening the spirits of all? That, I fear, is not the subtlety of the Way!” Tan Changzhen answered: “A chilled heart is not the Way, and a deluded man is not subtlety! Yet to be able to chill the heart—no one can say that is without the Way. To recognize delusion—no one can say that is without subtlety. Thus he does not speak of the Way’s subtlety, yet the Way’s subtlety is caught within it! For those who do not judge by victory and defeat, what spirit is there to dampen?”

Hao Taigu said: “What Brother Liu says does not stop here; there must be another reason.” Tan Changzhen laughed: “Exactly so! Exactly so! Brother Liu went to the banquet at the Jade Pool, stole a look at the fairy maidens, and the Queen Mother, angered, sent him down again to the mortal world. We two met along the road, and he told me of it. I answered him with the testing of the path by charcoal, and the advice of Jingyang. When he heard my words, he was set on going.”

Tan Changzhen stopped speaking here. Wang Yuyang asked: “What is he so bent on doing?” Tan Changzhen said: “He wishes to go among the painted women to awaken to the Way, in the grounds of silk and strings to probe the mystery, exercising his effort all the more so as to empty form and appearance.” Wang Yuyang said: “That which is seen but not perceived, heard but not heard—naturally there is no form or appearance.” Hao Taigu said: “It would be better to forget both self and other, and form and appearance will empty themselves.” Liu Changsheng said: “The words of you two can only be practiced by the highest and most accomplished. I now wish to take much seeing as my subtle function, and broad acquaintance as my practice.” Wang Yuyang and Hao Taigu both said: “Those who have subdued the demon of the senses abound from ancient times to now, but we have never heard of such a subduing as this.” Tan Changzhen said: “The resolute may turn to skill, the unresolute may hold to simplicity; each has its own subtle function, and there is no need to speak of it deeply.” When they had finished, the sky had turned late, and the four sat in meditation within the pavilion through the night. By the next day they parted and went their separate ways.

Turning alone to Hao Taigu: as he traveled along the road to Huayin, he looked up and suddenly saw a towering mountain, shaped like a hand, rising into the clouds. On the earlier journey escorting his master back to the west, the coffin had pressed upon his shoulders, and he had no chance to gaze about, so he had never seen this mountain. Now, free and without a care, he could from time to time admire the mountains and the waters along the way. The moment he laid eyes on it his heart was filled with admiration. He recalled his master’s words: “The place you see is the place where the Way is fulfilled.” So he climbed to its summit and saw the ten thousand mountains bowing and rising, all of them below it. Of old, Lord Kou Laigong had a poem saying:
Naught but the heavens hang above, No mountain can its equal prove;
Raise the head and the red sun is near, Turn and the white clouds below appear.

It turned out that this mountain was the immortal peak of the Western Marchmount, Mount Hua. Upon the mountain were more than ten palaces and shrines, all with Daoists burning incense and offering fire before them — a great deal of bustle. Hao Taigu looked about for a quiet spot. Having once learned the stoneworker’s craft, he went and made himself a hammer and a chisel, applied his subtle skill, and carved out a cave in the stone wall, just large enough to hold his knees. Just as he was about to enter the cave for quiet cultivation, there suddenly came a fellow Daoist, a cushion on his back and a spade in hand, who asked Hao Taigu to give up the cave for him to sit in meditation. Before Hao Taigu could reply, he walked straight into the cave, spread his cushion, and sat down to meditate, caring not whether he was willing or not—he had taken the cave first. Hao Taigu was a soft-hearted, tender man, and he could only say nothing and let him have the cave. He went further up and saw beside the path a great rock several fathoms tall. He hewed at this rock and wore out his hands and feet before he made a cave. It was somewhat roomier than the first, and he was greatly pleased. But lo, another fellow Daoist came, saying he had nowhere to sit; would the elder not be compassionate and give the cave to him. As Hao Taigu was a cultivator, he fulfilled the man’s wish and let him have the cave too. One after another across more than ten years, at the cost of endless hardship, he carved seventy-two caves—and seventy-two men came, and each by his entreaty had him give it away.

Still there was nowhere for Hao Taigu to cultivate. He searched over the rear of the mountain and found a spot. A cave could be carved there, yet it lay within a stone wall ten thousand fathoms high, a place where even a swallow could not fly. If he made a cave there, then however high a fellow Daoist might fly, he could not reach it. Yet there was no road to it—one must drop down by rope and be hauled back up by rope. Hao Taigu looked it over, went down the mountain, and with the alms he had gathered over the years bought a long rope; along the way he took on an honest disciple. Master and disciple climbed the mountain together and tied the long rope to a great tree. With his drill and chisel, holding the rope, his feet braced against the stone wall, Hao Taigu descended slowly until he came to the place. In between there was a little ledge where he could sit and stand, and there he worked at carving the cave every day.

That honest disciple prepared his meals. Hao Taigu ate but once a day and would not return until evening. The honest disciple grew weary of the cooking and thought to himself: “I thought learning the Way would be quiet and easy; who would have thought it would fall on me to cook, and with such hardship! What profit is there in my coming to learn the Way?” His mind then turned to evil, and he secretly carried a firewood knife at his side. Knowing that Taigu would go carve the cave after eating, he followed behind. He saw Taigu grasping the long rope, just as he was letting himself down. The honest, loyal disciple drew out the knife and with a single stroke cut the rope. The long rope sprang back, and down he fell over the ten-thousand-fathom cliff—no one knew whether Hao Taigu lived or died. Among the people of today there are meddlesome ones who have written four lines upon the cave wall of Ancestor Hao. What four lines, you ask?
A gentleman, take care, take care; Nine li and three tenths down, beware!
Should a man plunge from Huayin’s height, To Nanzhou come to seek his corpse aright.

Now it was that the honest disciple cut the rope with a single stroke of the knife and sent his master plunging down the ten-thousand-fathom cliff. He was certain the man must be dashed to pulp, so he gathered up his bedding and baggage, shouldered the whole of it, and set off. Down the front of the mountain he went for ten li or so until he reached a great rock. There he saw a man coming up from the foot of the mountain, who looked like his master; looking closely, was it not he? Startled out of his wits, with sweat streaming down his back, he met him head on and could not but cry out: “Master, where have you been?” Hao Taigu smiled faintly. “It is only that this drill of mine had gone blunt, so I went to the home of the blacksmith Wu of Shangzhou to
juān

(sharpen) it. And you, shouldering your bundle alone, where are you bound?” The honest disciple answered: “I saw that master had not returned for a long while, so I came here especially to meet you.” Hao Taigu laughed heartily: “What a filial disciple you are! Master was gone barely an hour, and you were so concerned that you shouldered your pack and came to meet me. There are another eleven or twelve li of mountain road, and the sun is but three fathoms high—how could you reach it? Had you not brought my bedding, I would surely have gone cold tonight.” And so saying, Hao Taigu went on ahead.

Leaving the disciple beneath the great rock, he turned the matter over and over in his mind: this master of mine—I truly do not know what sort of man he is. A cliff this high could not kill him. Perhaps his hardship is not yet done, and he must again spend his strength in carving caves, and cannot be free. And then he thought: could such behavior mean that he has become an immortal? If not, how was it that he could not be killed, and returned so quickly? What is more, when he saw me he only smiled and bore no grudge—he must indeed be a man of great magnanimity. If I let this master slip away now, under all the heavens I will not find a second one so compassionate. Most likely it is my own fault. Better that I go back up and serve him, and see whether there is a way for me to rise in the end. So he followed after him and said, when he saw his master: “The rope is cut; how can you go carve the cave again?” Hao Taigu said: “That is no matter—let me but leap down.” And so saying, he leapt, and flung himself down the ten-thousand-fathom cliff. If you would know what came after, wait for the next chapter to unfold.
My body is light and swift as a flying cloud; What fear the cliff of ten thousand fathoms proud?

blocks.text: 20. In the World of Gauze and Powder, Refining Form and Appearance; Uttering a Wondrous Gatha, Keeping the Thought of the Way Pure and True

inline.s: To see beauty as if none were there, the heart sits still, When one’s practice comes to this, it deepens of its will;
Whoever learns the Dharma of true emptiness, His tiger’s roar and dragon’s cry outrun all ages’ stress.

As the story says, Hao Taigu was a man who had attained the Way—how could he be toppled by a fall? When the disciple cut the rope, he had already shed his mortal body; now he was only coming to show a little of the Way, so that the people of later ages might know that the immortals can indeed be learned. When that disciple saw his master leap from the stone wall, his heart was filled with dread. He waited several days, and seeing that he did not come up, each went his own way.

As the story says, Liu Changsheng was wholly set on subduing the demon of sensual form. Hearing people say that the two cities of Suzhou and Hangzhou were full of beauties, he headed there at once. He picked up a few lumps of stone and turned them into gold and silver. Doffing his Daoist robes, he bought a few suits of silk and satin garments and dressed himself in them. Swaggering, he walked into the houses of pleasure, and the madam received him and could not but ask about his business. Liu Changsheng said to her: “My name is Changshengzi, a man of Yanshan, come here to purchase jewels. I have been long away from such pleasures and wish to find the very best young lady to ease my mind.”

When the madam heard he was a dealer in jewels, she knew that the God of Wealth himself had arrived. She broke into a smile, doubled her flattery, and led him straight to the room of a young lady of surpassing beauty. This young lady was named Siyu, counted among the famous courtesans of the pleasure quarters. She could play, sing, dance, write, paint, and compose a few lines of verse; graceful and winsome. When Siyu saw Changshengzi, his bearing was open and free and his speech gentle and warm; moreover he was open-handed and easy, with no trace of a stingy heart. How could a patron so generous not be entertained? So she gave free rein to every tenderness and a hundredfold allure, playing sweet and coy. But Changshengzi held to those two sayings of Master Chongyang: “When Mount Tai crumbles before you, be not startled—not that you make yourself not startled, but that before you it is as if it had never crumbled; when a beauty stands before you, be not moved—not that you make yourself unmoved, but that before you it is as if she were not there.” Holding to these two sayings of his master, he emptied his heart and mind, leaving them wholly void and empty, so that the demonic hindrances could find no way in. In vain the young lady lavished her thousand graces and ten thousand charms; she could not stir his heart.

This heart is the master of the whole body; when the heart does not move, the body is still of itself. All other thoughts and intentions follow the heart’s disposal, and when the heart does not move, they dare not move either. Only the eyes and the ears are two meddlesome beings: when they see a lovely color or hear a sweet sound, they come to report it to the heart. Changshengzi coaxed this heart well, telling it not to believe the words of the ears and the eyes, lest they wreck what mattered greatly. The heart indeed followed his words and made itself as one knowing nothing and perceiving nothing, like a little child that knows only to play and nothing of the passions of love. Lying in the same bed, sharing the same pillow, it was after all nothing more than a stinking bag of skin keeping company with a painted skeleton—no great joy in it. Only the reds and greens could not help but meet the eye; the tinkling and the clanging could not help but meet the ear. So Changshengzi coaxed the eyes and the ears as well and taught them a method: to see as if not seeing, to hear as if not hearing. And the two truly followed his method—one pretended blindness, the other deafness; and though they rose and lay with the young lady, in the end they still did not know what sort of person she was, nor what rare words she had to say.

As the story tells, because Changshengzi had coaxed these three elders—the master of the heart, the eyes, and the ears—they kept watch over him in the house of pleasure, and he there perfected himself into a true immortal. Now he was no longer so particular about his bearing, and would often play in the rooms of the courtesans. Seeing that he was willing to spend his silver and made no crude demands, which of them would not romp with him? So all day long there was teasing and laughter. And then one day, several courtesans came bringing flowers to Siyu, and they saw Changshengzi sitting shoulder to shoulder with the young lady. On a whim they pinned a fresh flower in Changshengzi’s hair, and then set about taking off his man’s clothes to dress him in woman’s apparel, unbuttoning the clasp at his breast. Suddenly they heard a cough from outside, and in burst a foreign monk. His face was dark, his beard short, his eyes large, his brows coarse, his forehead arched, his nose high—his looks altogether strange. The courtesans were so frightened that they hid behind Changshengzi and dared not make a sound.

Who was this foreign monk, you ask? It was none other than the ancestral founder Bodhidharma of the Western Land, returning from his wanderings by the South Sea and passing through Hangzhou. He saw a purple mist rising into the sky from within the house, which betokened the descent of a true immortal to the earth—and yet why should he be lingering among the pleasures of the flowered halls? He wished to come and awaken him, and to ferry him across. When he entered the house, the courtesans were just now in a hubbub with Changshengzi, pinning on flowers and stripping off his clothes. The madam of the house was bending over, tidying the chests, and the rest of the courtesans were napping in their own rooms. He heard the sound of laughter behind and burst straight in. Changshengzi saw him with a single glance, knew him for a man of extraordinary powers, and hurried to rise and show him respect, inviting him to sit. He noticed a copper kettle on the table, and the water in it was cold, so tea could not be brewed. There was no time to heat it upon a fire, so he snatched up the kettle and set it upon his belly, applying the work of inner fire. In an instant the kettle began to roar within and hot steam burst from the spout. Knowing the water was at a boil, he took a pinch of the finest downy tea leaves, put them in a teacup, poured the boiling water over them, and offering the cup in both hands, presented it to Bodhidharma. The courtesans, seeing this strange wonder, could only stare blankly and all cry out in astonishment.

Changshengzi laughed: “This is but a spark of true fire from among the Five Elements; what is there to wonder at? I can even bake cakes and griddle flatbread upon my belly.” The courtesans would not believe it; some went to fetch flour and others to fetch water. In a moment they made a cake as large as a bowl’s mouth and brought it for Changshengzi to bake. He took it in his hand, laid it upon his belly, and turned it round three times to the left and three times to the right, and the cake already took on a baked color. Turning it over, he turned it several more times, and the cake was done; he handed it to the courtesans. And those women tore a piece here and pulled a piece there, and ate the cake up.

Bodhidharma was a man who had seen the whole world as empty; he set nothing at all upon his heart, never in his life contended with another, and possessed complete cultivation and boundless compassion. Were he some shallow-minded fellow, would he not have made a show of his own powers? He was wholly unmoved, and instead put on a look of simple innocence, saying: “This trick of yours is quite amusing. When I come again I must learn it from you.” And so saying, he bowed and took his leave. As he was going he spoke four lines: “Since you know the road that comes from the east, / Let not the westward return go amiss; / Do not darken your true nature, / Nor linger in love and forget to go home.” When Liu Changsheng heard this, he too answered in four lines: “Empty, empty—not a single thing, / How could a thought go astray? / Who is the master of this body, / And where is my home?” Hearing these four lines, Bodhidharma knew him for a man of genuine cultivation. He said no more and drifted away.

It is also told that Yuyang came south, because at Ku County, Changsheng had spoken with him of the Way and told him he was going to Suzhou and Hangzhou to subdue the demons of the senses. More than a year had passed since their parting, and he feared that Changshengzi, dwelling among the pleasures, might lose his true nature. So he came to look for him, meaning to urge him to return early to the hills and the forests. That day he arrived in Hangzhou and searched several houses without finding him. As he was passing by, he saw two women with pomaded hair and powdered faces standing at a door. He walked up to them, meaning to ask where his friend might be. The two courtesans, seeing him come up, asked with a smirk: “Could this Daoist be coming to see that patron who griddled flatbread on his belly?” Wang Yuyang, thinking these words strange and suspecting that Changsheng was within, answered offhand: “It is exactly he whom I have come to see.” One of the courtesans said: “Since you have come to see him, come with me.” And so saying, she went inside, with Wang Yuyang following behind. How did those two courtesans know his intention? Because the day before they had seen a foreign monk in a wide-collared robe with a spade in hand; now they saw Yuyang also wearing a wide collar and carrying a spade, and guessed that he had come to see that patron. They expected another trick to be played and were glad of a chance to watch, so they led him in. As they drew near the door of the house, they suddenly heard the madam calling out, and the two of them left Yuyang and went off by themselves.

Wang Yuyang saw that the door of the room was half ajar, pushed it open with his hand, and indeed saw Changshengzi sitting beside a corsage of a beauty, dozing by the bed. At the sight Yuyang could not help laughing. On the table was a tube of tinder; he took it up, tapped the fire alight, and blew it toward Changshengzi’s face. The sparks of the fire flew every which way, landing on the young lady’s face and scorching her delicate flesh. Startled awake, she brushed wildly with her sleeve and cried out: “Who is it here that plays with fire and burns a person?” Changshengzi laughed: “The demon king is playing tricks on me.” Wang Yuyang also laughed: “It is I who play tricks with the demon king.” Changshengzi replied on the spur of the moment: “Call me a demon and a demon I stay, / One demon self can keep regret away; / You’ve blown your fire upon a lovely face, / Compare us then—whose demon holds more grace?”

Wang Yuyang was about to converse with him, when Liu Changsheng said: “Go quickly! Make haste! There is someone waiting for you in the land of Chu, and there you may together reach the far shore of the Way.” Wang Yuyang asked: “Brother, when will you leave?” Changshengzi said: “When the time comes I will go; I need not fix a day.” Hearing that his words had a meaning, Yuyang gave a slight bow, left the house of pleasure, and set out for the land of Chu. On the road he met Tan Changzhen, and the two agreed that running about was of no avail, while quiet cultivation had its merit. The two entered together the Cloud-Dream (the Yunmeng marsh, a great lake of antiquity; in ancient Jingzhou it was larger than the Dongting Lake of today; as the poem says: “The breath of the Cloud-Dream marsh, / The waves that shake the walls of Yueyang”), and cultivated there for several years until they attained the right fruit. Tan Changzhen wrote the “Cloud and Water Collection,” and Wang Yuyang wrote the “Cloud and Light Collection.” Tan Changzhen ascended on the first day of the fourth month, and Wang Yuyang on the twenty-fourth day of the fourth month.

It is also told that Changshengzi, having in the house of pleasure emptied form and appearance, left Suzhou and Hangzhou and returned again to eastern Lu, entering the hills for quiet cultivation. In the third year of Jiatai (the second era name of Emperor Ningzong of the Southern Song), in the guihai year, on the eighth day of the second month, he ascended. He left behind the “Collection of True Cultivation.” As for Hao Taigu, he cultivated for many years on Mount Hua, and on the thirtieth day of the eleventh month of the yichou year he ascended, leaving the “Collection of Taigu.” Among the Seven Perfect Ones, four had now concluded their lot. Only the affairs of Qiu Changchun, Ma Danyang, and Sun Bu’er remained unfinished.

Let us now take up Sun Bu’er. She had cultivated in bitter hardship in Luoyang for twelve years, and her great Way was accomplished, her transformations without end. She knew that Ma Danyang, keeping watch at home, would in the end find it hard to finish the Way, and she wished to return home and guide him. She also thought: I have been in Luoyang for many years, and everyone calls me a mad woman. If I do not show a little of the Way, how can I convert the hearts of the people? So she went out of the kiln, broke off two forked branches, blew a breath of true energy upon them, and cried, “Change!” The two branches became a man and a woman, and pulling and tugging each other, they went off into the city of Luoyang. When the townsfolk saw the mad woman linking arms with a nameless man, running up and down the streets, embracing shoulders and clasping waists, they were angry at being unable to shout them away or beat them off. Moreover Luoyang was a great city, a land of propriety and righteousness—how could it suffer her wild carryings-on? They discussed among themselves and decided to do away with the pair. But could they catch her, or could they not? Wait for the next chapter to unfold.
The streets from of old should quiet be; How can a man and woman roam so wildly free?

blocks.text: 21. Sun Bu’er Manifests Her Powers in Luoyang; Ma Danyang Meets a Friend West of the Pass

inline.s: Let not the six thieves assault you day by day, For every form and color is but empty clay;
Who wakes to find that from the first there is no thing, The spirit-tower dwells within this heart, its king.

As the story tells, Sun Bu’er transformed the two forked branches into a man and a woman whose resemblance was like her own. Every day they walked the streets with arms about necks and shoulders; beat them and they would not retreat, curse them and they would not go. At a loss, the neighbors joined together in presenting a petition: “We, the shopkeepers and people of the whole city, submit this plea that public morals be corrected and the streets made orderly. The matter is this: some years ago a crazed woman came from afar and took shelter in a ruined kiln outside the city. We, pitying her suffering, could not bear to drive her away, and gave her food and drink to keep her alive. Now this crazed woman is joined by a man, and every day they go about with shoulders embraced and necks entwined, laughing and playing. Repeatedly we have tried to drive them off and they will not go; it is truly an improper state of affairs. Luoyang is a great city, a thoroughfare between north and south—can it bear such foul disgrace and make us a laughing-stock to other regions? We humbly beg the clear-sighted magistrate to take charge and
tiǎn
(exterminate) this demon man and demon woman.”
The magistrate of Luoyang county, seeing this petition, pondered for a long while, then took up his brush and ruled:

What is called madness is the loss of one’s true nature. Such a one is thought to know nothing of human affairs, and so everything is pardoned. But by this petition, the nature is not lost—the madness is feigned. A man and a woman wandering together offends against propriety, and to clasp shoulders and embrace arms gravely wounds public decency. If they dare this in bright daylight, what they do by night need not be said. The streets are no place for pleasure, and a ruined kiln is no place for lewd display. Since they will not be driven away, their traces must be wiped out. Let us wait until
sì
(waiting) they have returned to their den, then spare not a cartload of firewood, raise the flame and burn it, that their kind be utterly cut off.”

When the ruling was given, the yamen runners made it known. The neighbors, receiving this verdict, each took up a bundle of firewood and made their way to the broken kiln. As they were walking along, they saw the crazed man and the demented woman going hand in hand into the kiln. With a shout, the crowd of neighbors flung the firewood into the kiln. In a moment it was piled into a mountain of wood. They set it alight, and up went blazing flames and flying sparks. Suddenly a thick column of smoke poured out from the kiln’s opening and turned into five-colored auspicious clouds, in the midst of which sat three immortals in meditation. The one seated in the center was none other than the crazy woman who had been raising such a ruckus in the streets. The crazed, demented woman said from among the clouds to the gathering of neighbors: “I am a cultivator, from Shandong, surnamed Sun, named Bu’er. I hid myself here in a feigned madness and cultivated for twelve years. Now that my great work is complete, I meant to use the fire to ascend, and so I turned these branches into a man and a woman to draw you here. Now that I thank you all for sending me off, I will see that the whole region stays at peace. I give this man and this woman to you as a token of proof.” And so saying, she pushed the two on her left and right down from out of the clouds, and they tumbled to the ground. The people hurriedly caught them in their hands and found they were but two forked branches; all broke out laughing.

When they looked again at the mad woman, she was already entering the Milky Way, her form growing ever smaller. In the turn of an eye they saw a black speck shoot straight up like a hawk, dwindling to the size of a coin, then of a bean, and then vanish. The people all faced the sky and bowed in worship. Indeed, for several years running the wind and rain came in season, and goods abounded and the people prospered. Grateful for her great virtue, they built a shrine of the Three Immortals, and whatever was prayed for was always answered.

It is also told that Sun Bu’er returned to the Ninghai county of Shandong and entered the manor, where Ma Xing caught sight of her at once and hurried over to welcome her. Sun Bu’er walked straight into the hall and sat down. Ma Xing went to inform the master, and Ma Danyang came out to meet her, saying: “Fellow Daoist Sun, you must have endured hardship.” Sun Bu’er replied: “Brother, why speak of hardship? This word ‘hardship’ is the very test of us who cultivate. One who cannot bear hardship—how can he cultivate?” As they spoke, the many servants came to pay their respects, and Bu’er comforted them with kind words.

That night they sat side by side in meditation. In the course of the night Ma Danyang had to get down several times, while Sun Bu’er sat without stirring. Ma Danyang said: “I see that Fellow Daoist Sun’s sitting skill is stronger than mine.” Sun Bu’er said: “Not only is my sitting skill a little stronger than yours, but my mystery is stronger than yours by tenfold.” Ma Danyang said: “Do not look down on me; I can turn a stone into silver.” Sun Bu’er said: “You can turn a stone to silver, and I can turn a stone to gold. But gold and silver cannot free one from birth and death nor make one an immortal; of themselves they are of no use. Of old, the Ancestor Lü Chunyang followed the Ancient Ancestor Zhongli to learn the Way. The Ancient Ancestor wrapped a thing in brocade silk, weighing a good many
jīn

(catties), and had Chunyang carry it upon his back. He bore it three years, wearing through both shoulders, yet never a word of complaint. At last, when the Ancient Ancestor bade Chunyang open the wrapping and look, it was but a stone; and even then Chunyang showed no anger.

The Ancient Ancestor said: “Though it be a stone, it can be touched into gold, so you have not carried it three years in vain.” And so saying, he pointed with his hand, and the lump of stone turned to gold. He said to Chunyang: “How would it be if I passed this art of touching stone into gold to you?” Chunyang asked the Ancient Ancestor: “Can the turning of stone into gold be guaranteed never to change again?” Zhongli, the Ancient Ancestor, said: “The gold so made is not the same as true gold. True gold remains the same from first to last, while the gold that is touched turns back to stone after five hundred years.” Then the Ancestor Lü Chunyang took his leave of the Ancient Ancestor, saying: “If that is so, your disciple would rather not learn it. This art yields its benefit for the five hundred years before, but leaves its harm for the five hundred years after—would it not wreck the people of the five hundred years to come? Therefore I do not wish to learn it.” The Ancient Ancestor Zhongli sighed: “Your resolve for the Way is beyond mine; the fruit you attain will be above my own.” Judging by this, this clever art of touching stone into gold can only do harm to later generations—what good is it to the Way?” These words left Ma Danyang silent and without a word.

On another day Sun Bu’er boiled a pot of water, carried it in a bucket into the room, and poured it into a bath basin, inviting Ma Danyang to bathe. It was the eighth month and the weather was still hot, yet the water gave off such steaming heat that one could not put a finger in. Ma Danyang dipped his hand in and was nearly scalded into blisters. He said over and over: “Hard to bathe! Hard to bathe!” Sun Bu’er said with a smile: “You have practiced for so many years, and you do not have even this little skill? Let me bathe.” And so saying, she took off her clothes and stepped in, stirring the water and splashing it about, showing no sign of the heat at all.

When she had finished bathing, she drew on her clothes and sat up. Ma Danyang said: “You and I study the Way under the same master and work in the same way. How is it that your arts are a match stronger than mine?” Sun Bu’er said: “The transmission is the same, but the refining is not. I practiced in bitter hardship in Luoyang for twelve years before I gained this mystery. You stayed at home enjoying ease and leisure, minding these few rooms, without stirring a single step. Unwilling to practice hard, afraid to leave your nest—how could you gain this skill?” Ma Danyang said: “After our master shed his mortal frame and ascended, no one was there to keep watch over the manor, so I did not venture far. Now that the Fellow Daoist has come home, it can be entrusted to her, and I too shall go out and seek the Way.”

That night he put on his Daoist robes and, at the first hint of dawn, while the others still slept, slipped out of the manor gate without anyone’s knowledge. Sun Bu’er saw that Danyang, having gone forth, was certain to attain the Way—of what use was all this wealth left behind? So she took it and used it to repair bridges, mend roads, and relieve the poor; she also adopted the son of Ma Ming to carry on the line of Ma Yu. When all matters were settled, she withdrew to the Jade Maiden Peak of Mount Tai and cultivated for several years, ascending on the nineteenth day of the second month.

It is also told that Ma Danyang, having left Ninghai county, did not know where it would be best to go. Then it suddenly occurred to him that his master’s grave was in Shaanxi—why not make a trip to Shaanxi? His mind made up, he set out west.

One day he reached Chang’an. Looking far off, he saw a fellow Daoist coming out of a village ahead, who looked just like Qiu Changchun. He thought to himself: “Whether he be or not, let me venture a shout.” So he called out loudly: “Fellow Daoist Qiu!” The man, hearing him, flew over as fast as he could, and indeed it was Qiu Changchun. The two met, exchanged greetings, and sat down together by the roadside. Ma Danyang asked him where he had wandered in these years and how his practice had fared. Qiu Changchun answered: “My master’s grave is here, and I could not bear to stray far; I have not dared to let my work of refining the nature go to waste.” Ma Danyang laughed: “Master had attained the great Way—how could he die? What is called death was only to cut off the deluded hopes of later people for becoming immortals; how could he truly have died! To refine the nature is inner work; to cultivate virtuous conduct is outer work. Master often said that only by cultivating both within and without can one be called truly wondrous. And you say you have not dared to let it go to waste—is that not mistaken?”

Hearing this, Qiu Changchun was suddenly awakened, and hastened to thank Danyang: “Brother’s words—through all my life I was in darkness, and by a single word I am now enlightened. It is truly the fortune of this humble Qiu.” He then recounted to Ma Danyang how, when escorting the coffin, he had seen the face of his master. Danyang said: “Master often said that you cannot hide your light and obscure your traces, that you insist on showing off your cleverness; your attainment of the Way will come after the other six. You must take heed of this now. If you will but examine yourself, hide your cunning and cleverness, and make your simplicity firm, then I will pass on to you in full the Way that my master transmitted to me.” Changchun, hearing this, was overjoyed, and led him to Dawan Village to pay homage at the Master’s shrine. They went also to the foot of Mount Zhongnan and paid respect before the grave-mound, and then traveled together through Jingxiang (that is, Jingzhou, so called because Xiangyang was its seat of governance).

Qiu Changchun deeply repented and reformed, hiding his form and concealing his traces, no longer showing off his cleverness. Ma Danyang indeed took the subtle mystery of the Way and guided him through it. Qiu Changchun diligently pondered the profound truth and dared not slacken. Seeing that the scenery of the land of Chu was lavish and extravagant, and not so plain and honest as Shaanxi, Ma Danyang traveled back with Changchun from the Xiang River up to the Xie Valley.

One day a heavy snow fell from heaven, and the two men were trapped in a cold shrine, sharing a single rush cushion to sit in meditation. Why did the two share one cushion? Because when Qiu Changchun had come to study the Way at the Ma manor, he had no Daoist implements at all. Later, when he went south of the Yangtze with Master Chongyang, Ma Danyang gave him a full set: the patched robe he had made, a rush cushion, and a spade. Later, when they escorted the master's coffin, the cushion was wrapped around the robe, laid on the coffin, and carried back across into Shaanxi. Over these years the robe had been patched again and again, but the cushion was still unbroken. Ma Danyang, meditating at home, had his own felt rug, so he had never had the cushion remade. And when they set out they had left in haste, carrying only a few changes of clothes and a few ounces of loose silver. By the time he met Qiu Changchun, that silver was all spent, and since then they had lived entirely on whatever alms Changchun could beg. One man's begging had to serve as the travel money for two, so how could there be any spare cash to buy a cushion? Hence the two shared this one cushion, sitting back to back in meditation. Those who cultivate the Way seek no ease at all; if only one can make do, the matter is settled.

Now to speak of Ma Danyang and Qiu Changchun meditating in the cold shrine of the Xie Valley. That night a great snow fell, level ground buried three feet deep. The Xie Valley lay among countless mountains, far from any dwelling, so that nowhere could they seek food; the two went hungry for three days and three nights. Suddenly a thought arose in Qiu Changchun — but you do not know what thought? See the next chapter for the unraveling.
Hounded by hunger and cold, hardship beyond words, how could it not make a man give rise to deluded thoughts?

blocks.text: 22. Dividing the Cushion, the Great Way Clings to No Affection; Asking Physiognomy, Judging a Man to His Face

inline.s: To do good is to climb a hundred-foot pole: coming down is easy, climbing up is hard.
Only diligently practice your merit and fruit, and let not the valor within your body grow cold.

Now Ma Danyang and Qiu Changchun sat in meditation in the cold shrine of the Xie Valley, blocked by snow so that they could not go out to beg alms. Qiu Changchun did not know that Ma Danyang was a man of the Way; he only pitied him for being born of a wealthy family — how could he bear such cold, such hunger and frost? Would that a bowl of gruel could be had to ease his hunger and thirst. He meant to go find some household and beg a bowl of alms to offer him.

Stepping out of the shrine he looked around, and saw only clouds barring the Qinling peaks and snow filling a thousand hills. Let alone a dwelling, even the trace of a road was buried under the snow, and he knew not where to set his foot. Were he to force his way on, he would surely tumble into a snowpit; not only would the gruel be beyond reach, his very life could not be preserved. Having looked, he came back into the shrine and sat down. Because he pitied Ma Danyang's hunger, this thought of a bowl of gruel stirred, disturbing his spirit and qi, so that his mind grew unsettled and he could not sit at ease. The whole night this thought troubled him, hard to still. It had already stirred the local earth spirit (
tǔ zhǐ

, the earth god), who hurried to the home of old Zhang in the mountain hollow to convey a dream. Zhang was sound asleep and dreaming when suddenly a white-haired old man walked in and said, 'In my shrine are two cultivators, blocked by the snow, who have gone hungry for three days and three nights. Hurry, rise and cook some rice and send it to them to ease their hunger and thirst.' When he had spoken he vanished. Zhang woke with a start, called his old wife awake and told her the affair. The old woman had believed in the gods all her life, and hearing these words she rose, lit the fire, and roused her son and daughter-in-law too. As they cooked the rice she told them her husband's dream, and the son and daughter-in-law were delighted. Soon the rice was cooked and the sky had brightened, and the old man was up as well. He bade his son bring the rice to the cold shrine and ask the two to eat. Ma Danyang thought that someone nearby, seeing them starve, had been moved to pity and sent the meal to relieve their hunger and thirst; so with Changchun he ate the rice. He spoke a word of thanks and still sat in meditation. When old Zhang's son saw them finished, he gathered the bowls and chopsticks and went off.

Ma Danyang sat until past noon, then rose and went out to look at the sky. Seeing a man coming from that direction, and fearing a troubling entanglement, he hurried back into the shrine. Just as he was about to sit, Qiu Changchun stood up and said, 'It seems that even cultivators are subject to influences and responses. Last night, fearing that you, elder brother, could not endure the hunger, a thought suddenly arose in me: how to get a bit of gruel to ease your hunger and thirst? That thought had no sooner arisen than this morning someone brought food — is this not a response?' Ma Danyang's face changed color and he angrily rebuked him: 'The noble man seeks the Way, not food. You give no thought to the work of advancing in the Way, but set your heart solely on food and drink. Have you not heard that the past mind should not be held, the present mind should not be kept, and the future mind should not arise? With these three minds not yet done away with, and a single thought not pure, how can you awaken to the Way? I will no longer travel with you; from this moment our mats are divided!' Hearing this, Changchun reproached himself for rising to the wrong thought and in gentle words tried to hold him back. While the two were in the midst of speaking, a man came outside the shrine. His firewood at home being burned up, he had come to cut the branches before the shrine. Seeing the woodcutter's cleaver in his hand, Ma Danyang asked to borrow it. The man, not knowing what he wanted, handed the knife to him. Ma Danyang took it, brought the cushion, cut it in two, and returned the knife. He said to Changchun, 'One cushion divided into two halves — take your half, I take mine, and each work his own merit. Do not be diligent at the start and idle at the end, and so ruin your own prospects.' Having spoken he went out and left.

Qiu Changchun would not let him go. He ran after him, but the woodcutter saw him and said, 'At this hour, where is the master going?' Asked, Changchun replied at once, 'I am going to catch up with my elder brother.' The man looked all around and saw no figure, saying, 'Where has your elder brother gone? I cannot see him.' Changchun pointed into the distance and said, 'He went off on this road.' The man said, 'For scores of miles this road has no trace of human smoke, and the sky is already dark; where will you lodge for the night? Better take my advice and stay one night, and go after him tomorrow, no later than that.' Changchun said, 'If so, you could help me call out a few times; perhaps if he hears me he will be willing to come back.' The man at once shouted from the tree, 'Master, come back quickly! You cannot go! You cannot go!' He called more than ten times, but there was no answer. He came down from the tree, gathered his firewood, and went home. Now Ma Danyang's fruit of the Way was already accomplished, and so he parted from Changchun, so that he might cultivate and refine himself and apply his effort. Had they stayed on the same road, it would only have delayed his prospects.

That day, once out of the shrine, he made use of the earth-concealment, and went straight to Mount Song in Henan to rest and cultivate. In the jiazi year of the Jiatai era, on the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month, he ascended in flight; he left behind a 'Record of Cultivating the True' to be handed down to the world.

Of the Seven Perfected Ones, six had already finished their work; only Qiu Changchun had not yet completed his cultivation. After Ma Danyang had divided the mat with him, he was all the more urged on, made several vows, and composed a verse for dispelling delusion, saying:
When deluded thoughts sprout they cannot be withstood: hungry, one longs for food; thirsty, one longs for soup;
Now put an end to all deluded thoughts at once, and exchange the old belly and bowels of former days.
[Nang (
nǎng
) shi] Nang shi means former times; of old.
To covet another's wealth, may your bones and sinews break; to crave another's food, may your mouth breed sores;
May every kind of delusion be wholly consumed, and within your body be utterly empty, with nothing hidden.

The verse was finished, and he rejoiced beyond measure. But after traveling for more than a month, he was bound to forget some of it. So he asked a carpenter's shop for a board and made it into a small plaque. He borrowed brush and ink and wrote eight lines on the plaque, so that whenever his eyes fell on it his mind would be struck with alarm. Do you know which eight lines?
To remove deluded thoughts, yet they are not cleared; now on this plaque I write them clearly;
Deluded speech and idle talk, remove them all; deluded fancies and greeds, sweep them all level.
To take money wrongly, may the hand be severed; to crave food wrongly, may the mouth breed sores;
At all times examine the affairs about you; do not let the seven emotions and six desires arise.

Qiu Changchun wrote the plaque and carried it by his side, and every day would read it once or twice. He took it thus: with every bit of delusion stilled, the practice deepens a step. By this effort of dispelling delusion he little by little refined it to maturity as he wandered east and west.

One day he came to the lands east of the River, and saw beside the road a neat, well-ordered country manor with its gate thrown open. It being high noon, he went to beg alms. He saw a young servant come out, and said to him, 'I have come from afar to beg a meal at this good manor.' The boy went back inside, and before long came out holding a tray of food, which he set on the stone block before the manor, and asked Changchun to eat. Changchun was about to eat when an old man of fifty-some years, half his hair white, came out. He gave Changchun a glance, took two steamed buns from the tray and gave them to him, and told the boy to carry the rest back in. Qiu Changchun, displeased, said, 'This lad brought the food to tie a karmic bond with this poor Daoist; why make him take it back in? Does the old gentleman begrudge it, or is this poor Daoist unworthy to enjoy it? Pray tell me plainly.'

The old man smiled and said, 'How could a bond of one meal be beyond this humble one to make? It is only that the master has not the good fortune to receive it.' Qiu Changchun, greatly startled, said, 'That I cannot receive even one meal — there must be a reason in it. I beg the old gentleman to instruct me plainly.' The old man said, 'From my youth this humble one has mastered the Mayi physiognomy, and has roamed the rivers and lakes for many years. When I judge a man's rise or fall, long or short life, prosperity or decline, I am never in the least in error. The rivers and lakes gave me a nickname, “Sai Mayi” (Rival of Mayi; the Mayi daoren was a Song dynasty master of physiognomy, said to have authored the book “Mayi Physiognomy”). Just now I looked at the master's physiognomy, and it is one that cannot eat its fill. If he eats one full meal, he will have to go hungry for several. So better give a little, and let him have something to eat every meal. This is this old one's good intention, not stinginess.'

Hearing this, Changchun nodded and said, 'The old gentleman has precisely named my failing, not a hair's breadth off. I pray you, sir, read my physiognomy afresh, and see whether my cultivation can accomplish the Way.' Sai Mayi indeed looked at him again and said, 'It cannot! It cannot! Do not blame this humble one for speaking plainly: in your face, at the tip of the nose, two lines divide and run to the mouth — this is called the Teng (
téng

) serpent sealing the mouth, and it foredooms one to death by starvation. Though the other parts of your face are fine, in the end you cannot escape this calamity. This calamity cannot be escaped, so how can you accomplish the Way?' Qiu Changchun said, 'Can it be changed?' Sai Mayi said:

Physiognomy settles a whole life; how can there be any change? Never until death does it end. Rich or poor, noble or lowly, in the world or out of it, if you are fated to starve, then starve you will; you cannot flee or hide, and there is no way to untie it. Let me tell you of two men of ancient times:

In the Warring States there was King Wuling of Zhao, whose physiognomy was one destined for death by hunger. He was a ruler of a state — how could he starve? Because his two sons fought for the throne and rose in arms. Fearing he had a partial heart, they first sealed the palace gates and set soldiers to guard them. The two sides hacked and slew at each other, for months on end without resolution. The palace provisions ran out, and the palace people all died of hunger. King Wuling of Zhao went hungry for seven days, not a drop of tea or water touching his lips. Seeing a sparrow's nest in a tree before the palace, he thought to take the fledglings and eat them. A long ladder stood by; he moved it under the tree and, summoning his strength, climbed up. But the fledglings had already left the nest, and only an egg remained. He took it in his hand and was just about to eat, when suddenly a big sparrow flew down and gave a flit of its wing. King Wuling's hand loosened, and the egg fell to the ground and broke. Because his physiognomy doomed him to starve, even a single sparrow egg could not be eaten, and he died of hunger at last.

There was also, in Emperor Cheng's time, an official named Deng Tong, whom a physiognomist said was destined to die of hunger. One day he saw Emperor Cheng and memorialized: 'Your subject Deng Tong, a clean and honest official, has no surplus in his house. The physiognomist says I am fated to starve; your subject reflects that his family is so frugal, and fears that in the end I may truly starve.' Emperor Cheng said, 'We can make men rich and can make men die; what are a physiognomist's words that they be taken as proof? We grant you the copper mountain of Yunnan to cast coins — in a year you may gain over a hundred thousand cash, and within ten years your household will be worth a million. How could you die of hunger?' Deng Tong thought he could escape starvation. But before long Emperor Cheng passed away, and the crown prince ascended the throne. The civil and military officials all impeached him for fawning on the late king and casting the state's copper coins for private use — no small crime. The young emperor, angered at the memorial, ordered his goods confiscated; and considering him an old minister of the late emperor, he could not bear to behead him, but cast him into the imperial prison. Then many officials memorialized again, and water and fire were cut off from him. He went hungry seven or eight days, and at the point of death asked for a mouthful of water. The jailer, stirred by pity, brought water; but the warden saw it and shouted, and the jailer's heart leapt in panic, so that he tripped and the bowl of cold water was spilled. Deng Tong died of hunger, not a mouthful of water drunk.

These two ancients, at the height of wealth and honor, ended in death by hunger — is this not proof that the physiognomy is accurate? This is why Boyi and Shuqi, who knew their fate, were willing to die beneath Mount Shouyang. Emperor Wu of Liang and Fu Jian, king of Later Qin, did not know their fate: one starved to death in the Terrace City, the other on Mount Wujiang. Whether one knows his fate or not, if he is destined to starve, starve he will in the end — how can he escape?'

When Sai Mayi had recounted these several ancients, Qiu Changchun was as though his very soul had been taken from him. In an instant his hot aspirations turned to cold ashes, and that whole mind bent on awakening to the Way melted and fell apart on the spot. At once he took leave of Sai Mayi, and no longer pressed forward, but returned to western Qin, his whole heart set on learning from the two worthies Boyi and Shuqi, to know their fate and obey heaven.

One day he came into the Qin lands. A valley opened between two ranges of high mountains, with a deep stream in the middle. On both banks of the stream lay jagged rocks in chaos; it was a remote mountain path, seldom traversed. He picked out a large rock, lay down upon it, and for seven days and seven nights went hungry, not drinking a mouthful of water, at peace with the thought of starving to death. Because he was a cultivator his spirit and qi were full, so he was not easily starved; an ordinary person would have been gone long ago. On the ninth day a sudden rainstorm fell, and the river swelled with a flood that soon crept up to him. He was a man seeking death, resolved to be at rest in his fate and trust to heaven so as to test the physiognomy, refusing to seek some other path to death; had he not been content in his fate but roused another thought and leapt into the water, how much suffering would he have saved? The ancients' mind held to one and did not waver, not shifting for life or death; therefore they are called truly genuine.

Now from upstream the water bore a fresh peach, big as a fist, bobbing to and fro on the current before Changchun, its fragrance wafting into his nostrils. Changchun had no mind to eat it, but thought: King Wuling, at the point of death, could not eat a single sparrow's egg; Deng Tong, at the point of death, could not drink a bowl of cold water. Now I too am at the point of death — I wonder whether I may eat this fresh peach? Whether Changchun could get to eat it or not — see the next chapter for the unraveling.
When fate does not doom one to die, in the end there is rescue; heaven sends a fresh peach to one's very lips.

blocks.text: 23. Transforming the Violent, Turning from Evil to Right; Speaking the Highest Principle, Gaining Life through Death

inline.s: Wealth and honor are from the first a bubble on the water; why must one ride a crane to Yangzhou?
There is a method of gathering the mind, that of the Lotus Pond; in stillness, secretly intone the 'One-Stroke Erasure.'
[Ou (
ōu
)] Ou means a bubble on water. [Yi bi gou] The Great Master Lianchi wrote the verses 'One-Stroke Erasure'; see in detail
The 'One-Stroke Erasure' (with annotation)

Now Qiu Changchun saw the water bring a fresh peach, and thinking that his fate doomed him to starve, feared that he could not have this peach. He thought, 'Let me try it and see what happens?' Reaching out, he took the fresh peach and bit (
dàn

, 'to eat') it. It was exquisitely fragrant and sweet, and after eating it his spirit rose greatly, and his hunger and thirst were at once resolved. The stream also subsided, and a round red sun shone high, baking him so that sweat ran over his whole body, so that he slept uneasily, and turned and rose. He reflected that his fate did not doom him to die by the waterside, but must be fulfilled on some high mountain. And he thought: with a single thought one falls under Mara, and for a whole life is bound in delusion. Therefore those who cultivate the Way must see the two words life and death as empty: one should not greedily cling to life, nor fixedly seek death. Let life be what it is, let death be what it is. One must not cling to being, nor sink into non-being. Thus Mara cannot enter the body, and the mind naturally attains stillness.

It is also said that Qiu Changchun came to the Qinling range, where he saw a small shrine on a mountain ridge, a wild and remote spot rarely trodden by men. He went in, spread his cushion, and lay down upon it. Again he went hungry for eight or nine days, not even drinking water. One day his life hung on a thread. Suddenly he heard people talking outside, and Changchun half opened his starving eyes to look. He saw a dozen or more persons sitting before the shrine, and saw a man walk in who looked at him and asked where he had come from. Changchun's mind was impatient; how would he trouble to answer with the whole story? His eyes held only a breath of life. Seeing him in this half-dead state, the man did not ask further, and went outside. With those others he looked for sticks and wood, propped a cooking pot on three stones, took out a large piece of meat from a basket, threw it into the pot, cooked it, and offered it to the god.

When the offering was done they cut the meat, stir-fried it, and poured it into an earthen basin, then boiled noodles and set out a bottle of wine. Calling each other brothers, they fell to eating and drinking. Do you know who these men were? They were highway robbers of the Qinling range, who stopped travelers and plundered them. Among them several heroes stood out: one called Zhao Bi, one Li Xiong, one Zhang Jian, one Wang Neng, and one Zhu Jiu. Having made a good haul, they had come partly to offer to the god and partly to divide the spoils, with wine and food. When the wine had half gone to their heads, Wang Neng said to Zhao Bi, 'Big Brother Zhao, we brothers have done evil all our lives; how say we do a good deed now?' Zhao Bi said, 'What good deed is there to do? Tell your elder brother, and I will see it carried out.' Wang Neng said, 'That old master collapsed in the shrine is not sick. To my eye he looks as though he has been starving. Why not boil some noodle soup and give it to him, and save his life?' Big Brother Zhao said, 'Good, good, good — brothers, go and do it quickly.' Hearing the big brother's order, those men set to with a flurry of hands and feet, and in no time the noodle soup was cooked. They came into the shrine and called Changchun to eat. He would not, but they lifted him, held his head, and poured two bowls down his throat. His belly was warm and full in a moment, and he came back to life, grumbling, 'Just as my great affair was settled, I meet you people, who feed me this nameless food and make me bear yet another hardship! Truly, once one cannot gain life, even seeking death costs much trouble.'

While Changchun spoke, Zhu Jiu's temper flared; he drew a steel knife from his waist and, in a fury, pointed it at Changchun and cursed, 'You wild Daoist, how foolish! We brothers saved your life, and instead you call it nameless food. Since you seek death, I'll give you a quick end!' So saying he raised the knife to cut. Qiu Changchun was unafraid; he patted his belly and said, 'Need not cut elsewhere — slit open my belly, and I'll draw out my own intestines to pay you back for your nameless food, and die content.' At this Zhu Jiu could not help laughing and said, 'You old master are without sense indeed — how can what's been eaten be returned whole? I won't kill you, but I'll ask why you seek death; speak it so we can all hear together.' Qiu Changchun then told them, 'Sai Mayi read my physiognomy as doomed to starve, never to change. Hence I am willing to learn from the two great worthies Boyi and Shuqi, to know my fate and obey heaven.' When Changchun finished, Big Brother Zhao said with a smile, 'Old master, you need not be so. Since you fear starving, let each of us club together a couple of ounces of silver — a dozen ounces in all. Go find a temple, take on a disciple, and lay up grain; how then would you starve?' Before Zhao Bi finished, Zhang Jian and Li Xiong each took out a few chunks of loose silver from their persons, about three or four ounces in all, and the rest also moved to take silver. Qiu Changchun shook his head and waved his hand, saying, 'No need. In all my life I have never wrongly taken another's wealth, and I have a plaque to prove it.' So saying, he drew out the plaque from his side and held it out for the crowd to see; on it were the lines, 'Take another's wealth wrongly, and the bones and sinews break; eat another's food wrongly, and the mouth breeds sores.'

Wang Neng laughed beside him and said, 'We brothers, with whole hearts, club together a few ounces of silver for you; it is not that you asked us for it. How is that wrong?' Qiu Changchun said, 'Whoever gets another's wealth without merit is said to be without cause; without cause means without reason. To take another's money and eat another's food without reason — how is that not wrong?' Zhu Jiu said, 'By the king's law one can beat a man to death, and by the Buddha's law one cannot live. When we brothers help you with a few ounces of silver, you dare not take it, afraid of some error; whereas we live entirely by robbery, and do not know how great our sin is.' Qiu Changchun said, 'Gentlemen, you are not like me. In my former life I never once gave help to anyone, hence in this life I cannot receive people's offerings. Gentlemen put out loans in former lives; those men swindled you of your wealth, so in this life when you meet them, you stop them on the road and exact the debt, returning it double. Had they not owed you, you would not have met them; and even if you had, you would have let them go lightly.'

These words of Qiu Changchun made the hair of the thirteen of them stand on end. Li Xiong said, 'How terrible, how terrible! If it is as this master says, does everyone owe us something? And might we not also owe something to others? If we owe others, then in another life they will stop us on the road and exact the debt; I fear we may never be able to clear it.' Zhao Bi said, 'We have a bit of silver on us, and could take up a small trade to get by. Let us seize this chance to turn from evil to right; what say you all?' Zhu Jiu said, 'The big brother's words are reasonable; let us gather in our hearts right now!' So saying, he flung the knife into the wild grass.
